#6459. The Gifts Chefs and Bartenders Actually Want This Year

Streetwear cooking shoes, a perfect pepper mill, and more

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

This is not your average “gifts for foodies” round-up. We know that you’ve probably been given a few too many wine glasses and cookbooks. “As a professional, I don’t want to be gifted introductory-level items that will ultimately go unused,” says Storm Brunni, private dining director at Barolo Grill in Denver. That’s why, for our guide, we’ve consulted you, the hospitality pros, about what you actually would like to receive this year.

New shoes for service. “I’m getting all of my favorite people the new high-top kitchen shoes by Chuck Taylor in leather anti-slip. They’re cool enough to complete your streetwear look, functional enough to wear in the dining room, kitchen, or work, and comfy enough to wear as a commuter.” —Jonathon Sawyer, chef at Kindling in Chicago

An industry-favorite hand cream. “Between constant handwashing, citrus, chiles, and hot pans, hospitality hands take a beating. Add a heated neck massager to use on the couch after a midnight close, and you’ve basically given someone a spa day.” —Antelmo Ambrosio, executive chef at Casa Oaxaca in New York City

Something for the coffee nerds. “It’s definitely a splurge, but I buy myself the Onyx Coffee Advent Calendar every year. A lot of hospitality pros nerd out about coffee, and Onyx is one of the best roasters. They fill the calendar with individual portions of beans (enough for two people) with different origins, roasts, and processes every day. Everything is roasted on a schedule so that when you’re brewing each one, the coffee is at its peak that day. The calendar has some of their signature coffees, alongside one-offs that you’ll never be able to get again, and I’ve tried some of the best coffees of my life in past calendars.” —Katie Renshaw, owner of Bar Bambi in Chicago

An upgrade for kitchen organization. “I love this automatic tape dispenser. Gift it with a nice fresh box of Sharpies.” —Kevin Beary, beverage director of Gus’ Sip & Dip, Kitty’s Cosmopolitan Club, Three Dots and a Dash in Chicago

The gift of longer-lasting produce. “Vejibag is a family-owned business, run by a small team of women who create 100 percent organic cotton bags designed to keep produce fresher for longer at home. They genuinely work and are an amazing addition to any kitchen.” —Lauren DeSteno, executive chef at Ai Fiori in New York City

A tool for operators who know there’s always something that needs fixing. “I was given a precision screwdriver from HOTO Tools and now I’m obsessed with the brand and their design aesthetic. So many things in the restaurants need little fixes all the time and the 3.6V Electric Screwdriver Kit Pro has all the bits you could need. I also love their rotary drill for polishing plateware with chips/scratches for work.” —Zach Engel, chef at Galit and Cafe Yaya in Chicago

Gifts with a personal touch. “As a general manager some of the top staff requests I’ve received are for nice wine keys (it’s an even nicer touch if they’re engraved) and custom server books.” —John Schneekloth, general manager at Toro in Chicago

Nice dishware is worthwhile at home, too. “I’d love to receive items from Ivo Angel, a beautiful ceramics company out of Italy. I am a huge fan of the splatter design and always want a pinch bowl; I can’t have too many. Also the olive bowl with an attached vessel for pits is perfect for hosting.” —Julia Jaksoc, chef and owner of Bar Roza, Cafe Roze and Roze Pony in Nashville

The pepper mill that chefs swear by. “It’s one of those tools that gets used constantly, makes a real difference, and is something every cook or bartender would appreciate having.” —Marco Torres, Chef at Brass and The Tusk Bar in New York City

Fun socks. “Being locked down in heavy black pants, unforgiving non-slip shoe leathers, and a stiff chef coat means you have to find your personality somewhere. A pair of loud, ridiculous socks underneath always makes me feel a little more human. I’ll never forget getting this pair of bright yellow Spam socks as a Christmas gift one year. Honestly, it’s one of the best presents I’ve ever unwrapped, and it brings a little joy each time I slip them on.” —Soo Ahn, chef/partner at Adalina Prime, Arla and Adalina Italian in Chicago

Something to take the edge off. “For the industry pro who enjoys a little puff puff and a good nap (especially after a Saturday morning shift with lines out the door), you can’t go wrong with Tokin’ Jew rolling papers. We sell them at the deli because, come on, but they’re also a fantastic gift. And for the pipe people, their pickle pipes are another way to keep it kosher.” —Jake Schneider, chef and co-owner of Schneider Deli in Chicago

A beautiful book for recipe writing. “I would gift this brown leather journal cover from Shinola along with this 12-pack of pens. I think the notebook is a worthwhile splurge, and while I know the idea of a more expensive and elegant pen is both compelling and sexy, it is also impractical for when you’re on the go or as prone to losing nice pens as I am. These ones write fluidly and beautifully.” —Róbert LeBlanc, creative director and founder of LeBlanc + Smith in New Orleans

The kitchen fit of your dreams. “I could wear this jumpsuit 24/7! It’s comfortable, easy to move around in, and perfect for those long days in the kitchen when I’m constantly running around and want something that looks as good as it feels.” —Andrea Belfiore, chef and founder of EVÈNTO in New York City

A tool for foraging. “I love my ARS pruning shears. I take them pretty much everywhere when I’m out foraging, and they’re great for everything from cutting herbs to collecting branches and other ingredients for drinks. They’re one of those tools I use all the time.” —Danny Childs, co-owner of Field Day in Philadelphia

A trio of pastry chef staples. “On any given day, a pastry professional will produce dozens of recipes, and we need tools to measure mass/weight, time, and temperature. Even when we have our own, backups or better ones are always welcome! My top picks include: this scale, which has a pull-out screen when you’re scaling on to sheet trays or large bowls; this kitchen timer has four color-coded channels for timing multiple projects at once; and this thermometer, which is fast-reading, accurate, and has a magnet on the back for easy access on any magnetic surface.” —Orlando Soto, executive pastry chef of Le Bernardin in New York City

The perfect vessel for an industry-favorite amaro (or 50/50 shot). “Some of the best hospitality happens in an ounce and a half: a pour of Cynar for a regular who had a long week, a welcome taste for someone new at the bar. I’d recommend these little ceramic artichoke shot glasses to make that moment feel even more considered.” —Steven Waters, owner and operator of Fino in Denver

Many knife options. Patrick Dooley of Harry’s Bar in Paris recommends Le Grand Tradi, which is sized between a paring and chef’s knife, making it a great workhorse option, while Nancy Santiago, beverage director at NYC’s IGC Hospitality, recommends a Japanese petty knife “for precise citrus work and garnish prep.” Amir Babayoff of Ophelia Lounge in NYC is partial to Tojiro’s chef knives.

And knife storage and upkeep options. Schneekloth of Toro recommends a knife backpack, while Devin Denzer, chef at Atsumeru in Chicago, recommends a whetstone and ceramic sharpening rod, especially for newer line cooks.

A thoughtful gift card. “Here are a few gifts that I have received that stood out to me: a hefty gift card to a sought-after restaurant with guaranteed reservations on a night off, which is such a good way to give someone a night out; a gift card to a shoe store that carries high-quality work shoes, like Red Wings, Dansko, or Blundstones; and a gift card to something wellness-related—my business partner Jesse got me three sessions at a body-stretching spa downtown.” —Phila Lorn, chef and co-owner of Mawn and Sao in Philadelphia

Responses have been edited and condensed for clarity.

A 2,000-year-old tomb was discovered in an elite burial ground of the Xiongnu, some of whom were the ancestors of the Huns.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have unearthed a massive 2,000-year-old tomb of an elite nomad from the Xiongnu Empire in Central Asia. The nine-level tomb contained more than 400 grave goods and is the largest Xiongnu tomb ever found in Mongolia.

Archaeologists identified the enormous tomb full of riches during a four-year excavation at the site of Duurlig Nars in northern Mongolia, according to a translated statement from the National Museum of Korea, whose researchers have been excavating the site in cooperation with the Institute of Archaeology of the Mongolian Academy of Sciences and the National Museum of Mongolia.

Duurlig Nars is the largest noble burial complex of the Xiongnu Empire, with nearly 300 ancient burial mounds called kurgans. The Xiongnu, also known as the Hunnu, were a collection of nomadic tribes who coalesced into a mobile empire on the Mongolian steppe in 209 B.C. The Xiongnu were connected to a broad trading network that stretched from the Roman Empire in the West to China and the Korean Peninsula in the East.

When the Xiongnu Empire fractured in the late first century B.C., one band moved west, picking up new tribes and eventually becoming the horde known as the Huns. Both the Xiongnu and the Huns were well known for their fighting and horseback riding skills.

The newly announced tomb is roughly square, with a long passageway extending from it, according to the statement. Including the passageway, the tomb is about 240 feet (73 meters) long, roughly the size of the Great Sphinx of Giza. Archaeologists discovered nine concentric layers of stone, each smaller than the last, going down around 48 feet (14.5 m) deep, making the tomb a kind of inverted pyramid.

Jade "bi" discs unearthed on the floor of the coffin.

A glass cup with a handle, possibly made in the Roman Empire.

Archaeologists unearthed a wooden carriage from one of the tomb layers.

In the tomb's central chamber, archaeologists found a wooden burial chamber with a coffin. The burial chamber is smaller than other elite Xiongnu burials, according to the statement, which may suggest that the society was changing and Xiongnu power was declining when the tomb was created in the late first to second century A.D.

Artifacts found in the tomb show the extent of the Xiongnu's connections across Eurasia 2,000 years ago, according to the statement. Among the grave goods recovered from the tomb were silver-and-quartz accessories crafted to decorate horses, as well as a wheel from a lacquered horse-drawn carriage, suggesting the tomb's occupant was a person of high social status.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Additionally, archaeologists found evidence of connections with the Han dynasty, which arose around 200 B.C. and was the second imperial dynasty of ancient China. On the bottom of the wooden coffin, archaeologists recovered 15 flat, overlapping pieces of jade.

Han dynasty burials of important people often included at least one "bi," the term for a jade disk. But unlike the typically circular "bi," the jade pieces in the Xiongnu tomb are irregular and have elaborate designs engraved on them, according to the statement. This may suggest that the Xiongnu adopted a Han burial practice but put their own spin on it.

Archaeologists also found a broken cup in the tomb. The transparent glass cup with a handle may have been manufactured in the Roman Empire, the archaeologists believe. Additional tests will be carried out to try to determine where the glass cup was made.

So far, archaeologists are unsure who was buried in the tomb. But they plan to use DNA analysis techniques on the teeth and hair they recovered from the coffin to figure out the person's chromosomal sex and whether the individual was related to other people interred in the Duurlig Nars burial complex. According to the statement, future analyses of this important tomb will help archaeologists paint a more detailed picture of ancient Xiongnu society two millennia ago.

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6457. Detecting Primordial Black Holes By The Stars They Destroy

Dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light. Scientists put their minds into hyperdrive trying to understand it and figure out what it is. One of the proposals is that primordial black holes (PBH) account for some or all of dark matter.

Primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Big Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter. Really small PBHs wouldn't have survived this long because of Hawking Radiation, but more massive ones could have. New research focuses on asteroid-mass PBHs and how they could be detected, if they exist.

The research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The lead author is Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT. The authors focus on what are called Hawking stars, stars that have engulfed a microscopic PBH. They're named after renowned physicist Stephen Hawking, who first proposed them in the 1970s.

"Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (1017â1023 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars," the authors write. Though it's all theoretical at this point, the researchers developed a framework for what would happen to stars that capture these PBH. They used stellar evolution models, simulations, and other tools to try to understand what would happen.

Primordial Black Holes are only theoretical, so far. But if they exist, they could find their way inside main sequence stars. Image Credit: NASA and G. Bacon/STSCI

First of all, a single star on its own is unlikely to capture a PBH. But a star with a stellar or planetary companion would have enough gravitational interactions to trap a PBH in one of the stars. It could take thousands or even millions of year for a PBH to work its way into a star's center.

âThen, this is where the action begins,â said lead author Gottlieb. Once the PBH reaches the center, the star can't survive.

According to this work, there are two outcomes for stars that suffer this misfortune, and both spell doom. "We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly," the authors write.

Once a PBH finds its way into the center of a star, it takes only a few million years before it consumes about 1% of the star's mass. Then, the rotation rate comes into play. If it's fast enough, the star's gas can't fall directly into the PBH. Instead, an accretion disk forms around the PBH, inside the star. This is where the two outcomes diverge.

âInside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,â Gottlieb said. This is an almost unimaginable scenario, but the research shows it's possible.

âThe black hole is also spinning, and itâs twisting space and time.â

The PBH then warps the star's magnetic fields, and just like in a SMBH, powerful jets are launched. âThis twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,â Gottlieb explains.

What star could survive powerful jets being emitted from inside?

âOnce the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,â said lead author Gottlieb. The authors write that this produces "an explosive Hawking-star transient powered by a rapidly spinning PBH." The PBH emits jets that tear through the star, quickly destroying it.

âAnd these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds," Gottlieb said. "Itâs very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.â

This schematic illustration shows the evolutionary sequence of a Hawking star. First the PBH is captured, and eventually it migrates into the stellar core. Once the PBH is embedded in the core, the PBH grows by accreting stellar mass. What happens next depends on whether the PBH forms a disk before it consumes its host. If a disk forms, that warps the magnetic fields, and the PBH launches jets from inside the star, destroying it in seconds. If no disk forms, the star dies a quiet, gradual death, and a stellar-mass black hole is left behind. Image Credit: Ore Gottlieb et al 2026 ApJ 1012 157

In the second case, the star's destruction is less cinematic. "The system dies quietly," the authors write, "leaving a PBH with mass of the order of the consumed stellar mass and little or no bright disk-powered emission." It's basically a stellar-mass black hole indistinguishable from others of its kind.

These two paths to destruction create different prospects for observing PBHs engulfed by stars.

"Our results carry important observational implications across both electromagnetic and GW channels," the authors explain. "If a PBH has grown sufficiently to form an accretion disk, the associated disk winds and relativistic jets can inject enough energy and momentum into the stellar envelope to unbind the star and power an explosive transient."

The rapid destruction creates a bright transient that emits EM radation across multiple wavelengths. This could be detectable at long distances with modern telescopes, similar to supernovae.

âWe would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,â Gottlieb says. âThis is something we could potentially detect, if itâs not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.â

This simulation depicts the moments after a primordial black hole is captured by a star. As soon as the black hole falls into the starâs center, it creates a swirling disk of material (orange). Within a matter of seconds, interactions between the black hole and the spinning disk should launch powerful jets of matter that ultimately pierce through the star, making it explode.

GWs from these events are likely more rare. Scientists have long wondered if PBH could be GW sources, and it's possible that the Hawking-star remnant that's left behind could be detected as one if it ever formed a compact binary with another compact object. The authors say that if this happens, it's exceedingly rare. But if it does happen, observing them would be very informative. "Thus, GW detections would be highly diagnostic if found, but should be regarded as a binary-evolution-limited and likely subdominant discovery channel for Hawking stars.

Here's where dark matter comes in. These Hawking-stars, if they exist and can be detected individually, could be used to calculate their population. If these stars work the way the researchers think they work, they can be detected and used to "provide independent observational constraints on the PBH population," the authors write. But on the other hand, "the absence of such transients or of convincing subsolar merger candidates could constrain the fraction of DM in PBHs."

So it seems there's a potential viable pathway to detect dark matter, if indeed PBHs are real and astronomers can find them destroying a star in a telltale blinding flash.

âThere is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,â Gottlieb said. âWe expect this to be visible, and itâs something we should look into.â

#6456. The Best Little Gifts Your Holiday Party Host Will Actually Want

Don’t show up empty-handed or with a cheap bottle of wine — bring status cocktail cherries, a beeswax candle, or a painterly placemat

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A good host is always thinking of others, whether it’s by making guests feel welcome, accommodating everyone’s diets, or setting an Instagram-worthy tablescape to make the night feel extra special. But the holiday season is an opportunity to flip the script and show the host you’re thinking of them, too. Bringing them a gift is the cardinal way to thank the host for all their thoughtful work. The only question remains: what to give?

For those who delight in trotting out their special dinnerware for guests, there’s a world of creative and whimsical gifts out there, even if it seems like they already have the entire CB2 catalog. And if that is the case, this just means you, as the gift-giver, can allow them to indulge in the things they typically would not. Take, for instance, some unique vintage shot glasses, intricately carved chopsticks, and pearl cocktail picks. Not only do these playful takes on essentials inspire joy, but they’re also sure to be conversation starters for future gatherings. And, as the bestower of the new treasured piece, you just might secure yourself the invite for the next one.

You can never have enough serving utensils if you love to host. That moment when you toss your pasta salad, plate everyone’s green beans, or dole out your main dish is an opportunity to flex some of your more decorative yet functional kitchen tools. This ethereal stainless steel set from Leif boasts pewter star-shaped handles with sea glass.

Even Diaspora Spice Co.’s everyday spices come in bold, ready-to-gift packaging, but the equitable spice company’s new holiday spice sampler gift box is an extra colorful treat for the senses. The bundle includes samples of its beloved Nandini coriander, a rare Ceylon cinnamon, a Himalayan foothills-sourced pink garlic powder, and several more spices to inspire your host.

When it comes to gift-giving, we believe in working smarter, not harder. Case in point: Buy a set of nice-looking vintage glasses — these are labeled shot glasses by the seller, but they’re just as nice for sipping cordials — and rather than giving one lovely host a set of eight, split them up into pairs or fours and use them for multiple gifting situations. There’s always a use for little glasses like this (and they’re pretty enough to display, too).

It’s pretty fun to use a posh plaid napkin when you’re digging into some quiche or sipping on mulled wine.

It’s always fun to kick off an evening of cocktails with a caviar bump, which is what makes this Imperia Caviar bundle such a gift for the avid party host. The 30-gram tin of royal ossetra comes with a mother-of-pearl spoon and a caviar tin opener in a velvet bag, and the bundle’s compact size means you can simply slide it into your purse or jacket on the way to the function (unlike a heavy bottle of wine or olive oil, which would likely need their owns bags).

It really has been the year of the dirty martini. For those who are building a bar cart (or want to start), getting a couple of sets of proper cocktail picks can be a game-changer. Nothing wrong with a traditional wood toothpick, of course, but it really does add a lot of pizzazz to a martini to bite the olives off a pearl-emblazoned skewer.

Swooning will abound once people get a look at these beautiful walnut chopsticks featuring inlaid geometric designs. Another great example of “practical, but nicer to look at than what you might get for yourself.” Plus, you can grab a set of five on sale right now for under $20.

When it comes to cocktail cherries, one brand truly reigns supreme: Luxardo, which has been making candied cherries soaked in marasca syrup for 120 years. A classic for a reason!

Jonathan Adler is another designer to keep tabs on when it comes to playful but elevated home decor. This set of Matisse-esque coasters also has a slight lip to keep condensation from spilling, and would be prime for serving up lychee martinis the next time you gather with friends. Snag them while they’re 40% off for Black Friday.

Halen Môn is a salt nerd’s dream. The organic, hand-harvested sea salt hails from the tides of the Isle of Anglesey in Wales (Halen is Welsh for salt; Môn is Welsh for Anglesey), and has earned numerous awards for its subtle crunch and crisp mineral flavor. Any host would be thrilled to receive a bag of the stuff, but this gift set combines the salt with a charming ceramic cellar and spoon.

Matches are always a solid host gift, and a small but useful present that’s made all the better with cool packaging. The lifestyle brand State the Label, for example, has housed its matches in a folk art-inspired cottage (the striker paper is on the bottom of the house).

Those who like to entertain likely appreciate a good placemat. This set of two block-printed placemats from West Elm puts a romantic spin on the dining-table staple with painterly tones and bright hues. Who wouldn’t love to receive these dreamy accents?

Is your host a lover of ice-cold martinis? Perfect gift incoming: Quincy’s fabulous olives, which have superb flavor and are ratioed with drink-perfect brine to make exactly 14 dirty martinis per jar.

Scents are tricky. Unless you really know your host, refrain from gifting them scented candles, and opt for a beeswax pillar candle instead; they can light it sans candelabra (unless you’re sure that they own one and prefer tapers) by simply placing it on a small plate. Above all, beeswax candles make a wonderful dining companion, because they don’t emit the same stuffy, paraffin wax-based smoke as non-beeswax candles.

Sometimes, brevity is wit. Give it to someone who means business, or orders the business women special.

We all love a little Le Creuset in our kitchens, but a Dutch oven isn’t in the price range for what we’d consider an easy host gift. Enter the butter dish, a fabulous little thing to present and say “I brought you something,” presented with a kiss on the cheek and maybe a bouquet of flowers or bottle of wine.

#6455. Psychedelics May Leave a Lasting Mark on the Brain, New Research Reveals

What remains in the brain after a psychedelic wears off could matter for future medicines, as rat scans revealed distinct activity patterns a week after three different drugs were given.

Psychedelic drugs are attracting growing interest as possible treatments for depression, anxiety, and addiction. Yet new research suggests that drugs often grouped together under the same label may affect the brain in very different ways, potentially influencing how scientists investigate their medical uses.

Researchers at the University of Southern Denmark compared three psychedelic drugs, LSD, psilocybin, and the synthetic compound 2C-B, using brain scans in rats. They examined changes in brain activity while the drugs were active and again one week later, after their immediate effects had worn off.

Unlike earlier studies that largely examined one psychedelic at a time, the direct comparison revealed distinct patterns for each drug. Only a few changes were shared across all three.

“Psychedelic drugs are often discussed as if they work in the same way. But when we look at the brain, the differences are clear. Each drug appears to affect its own networks, and that is new knowledge,” says Mikael Palner, Associate Professor at the Department of Clinical Research at the University of Southern Denmark and senior author of the study.

While the drugs were active, LSD and 2C-B produced the greatest number of changes in brain activity. The researchers also identified different patterns one week later, suggesting that the effects of these substances may extend beyond their immediate action in the brain.

“What is interesting is that the differences do not only appear while the drugs are active. We can also see different traces in the brain afterwards. 2C-B mainly affected areas linked to reward, LSD affected areas linked to habits and motivation, while psilocybin stood out by primarily affecting areas involved in emotions,” says Frederik Gudmundsen, first author of the study.

Gudmundsen completed his PhD at the University of Southern Denmark and is now a postdoc at the Department of Clinical Medicine, Translational Neuropsychiatry Unit, Aarhus University.

These differences could help researchers investigate whether certain psychedelics are better suited to treating particular conditions. However, the brain activity patterns alone cannot establish which drug, if any, would be more effective for a specific disorder.

“If the drugs affect the brain differently, it is also possible that they may eventually prove better suited to different disorders. We do not know that yet, but our study provides a biological starting point for investigating it,” explains Palner.

Several psychedelic drugs are already being investigated in clinical trials for conditions including depression, post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), and addiction. Understanding how individual substances affect different brain networks could eventually help scientists develop more targeted approaches to treatment.

For now, the findings remain limited to experiments in rats and do not show whether the drugs are effective in patients. Further research in humans will be needed to determine whether the same differences occur in the human brain and whether they can help guide future psychedelic treatments.

Reference: “Serotonergic psychedelics induce distinct patterns of metabolic activity and covariance within biologically informed rat brain networks” by Frederik Gudmundsen, Julia Czurylo, Daniel R. #6454. New Research Reveals Europa's Sodium Cloud Originated from its Interior Ocean

Jupiter's moon Europa has been fascinating astronomers and astrobiologists for decades. Ever since the Voyager probes passed through the system in 1979, scientists have theorized that an ocean lies beneath its icy crust. Further observations bolstered this theory, revealing surface plumes caused by warm water pushed up through vents in the crust (cryovolcanism). They've also found fascinating chemistry on the moon's surface, and an enormous, diffuse cloud of sodium surrounding it.

And now, observations by the W.K. Keck Observatory in Hawai'i have revealed something new and very surprising. That sodium cloud has remained remarkably stable after more than two decades of observations despite the dynamic and powerful forces that characterize Jupiter's environment. In a recent study led by Boston University, an interdisciplinary team of researchers compared sodium measurements high above Europa with observations of sodium clouds very close to the surface.

Their results, reported in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, provide the first connection between the two, giving scientists a more complete view of the moon's environment. This, in turn, gives scientists a sneak peek at the ocean beneath Europa's surface. The team's observations relied on two decades of observations using Keck's High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) instrument, allowing them to map the sodium cloud's distribution and how it responds to changing conditions in the system.

Europa's sodium cloud is oblong-shaped, elongated in the east-west direction, and measures over 46,800 km (29,095 mi) in diameter, or about 30 times Europa's radius. Sodium is of particular interest to planetary scientists because it is a constituent of sodium chloride (salt), a key ingredient in Earth's oceans. Based on the latest fossil evidence, scientists theorize that life first emerged approximately 4 billion years ago in Earth's primordial oceans around hydrothermal vents.

Based on multiple lines of evidence, astrogeologists also believe that similar vents exist inside Europa at the core-mantle boundary. Understanding the origin and distribution of sodium around Europa can help researchers learn more about the materials on the moon's surface and potentially subsurface. Emma Lovett, a graduate student at Boston University and lead author on the study, explained in a W.M. Keck Observatory release:

We don't know a lot about Europa's hidden ocean and icy surface, but its atmosphere offers a window into this potentially habitable world. The whereabouts of life beyond Earth might be closer than we ever imagined.

However, studying sodium close to the moon's surface presents many challenges. Foremost among these is the highly reflective nature of Europa's surface ice, which can overwhelm the faint signal emitted by nearby gas. To overcome this problem, the team used the HIRES instrument's high-resolution, long-slit configuration to measure the sodium's distinctive spectral fingerprint. They also observed Europa as it passed through Jupiter's shadow, ensuring that there was no direct sunlight reflecting off the surface to interfere with the signals they detected.

By changing the instrument's orientation at multiple locations, the team mapped the sodium cloud rather than measuring its spectra at any single point. Lastly, they combined new observations with archival data Keck obtained in 1999 to see how the cloud changes over time. Surprisingly, they found that the cloud has remained stable despite changes in Jupiter's plasma environment and the influence of the neighboring volcanic moon Io, which spews sodium into space. Said Carl Schmidt, a researcher at Queen's University Belfast and Boston University:

The neighboring volcanic moon Io sprays sodium around the Jupiter system, and we've often wondered if Io paints Europa's surface. The stable sodium abundance in these Keck data shows that Europa is indifferent to Io's volcanic activity. What we observe originates in Europa's saltwater and not in Io's volcanoes.

Radiation from Jupiter can break apart molecules on Europa's surface. This can free oxygen, which could percolate in brines through the surface into the ocean under the ice. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech

A particularly beneficial observation occured on September 29th, 2022, when NASA's Juno spacecraft passed behind the moon relative to the team's perspective. For the past ten years, Juno has studied Jupiter's atmosphere, magnetosphere, and plasma environment. So on this occasion, the team had the chance to study the sodium cloud alongside measurements of the local plasma cloud. This enabled the team to examine the sodium cloud across a range of conditions and to test the effects of Jupiter's magnetosphere and Io's volcanic activity.

While most astrobiology missions are currently searching for evidence for past life on Mars, Europa is the next target in the search for extraterrestrial life. Right now, NASA's Europa Clipper mission and the ESA's JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) are en route to the system to study this icy moon. Because Europa is not a terrestrial planet but an "Ocean World," it offers major opportunities to study potentially habitable environments beyond Earth. In particular, scientists want to see how water and other materials are transferred between the surface and the interior.

While no direct evidence of organic molecules has been detected on the surface, research strongly indicates the moon has the key chemical ingredients and pathways to form them. And while the sodium cloud does not provide a direct measurement of Europa's ocean, understanding its origin and behavior helps scientists understand the moon's chemical environment. Building on their momentum, the team is currently using the Hubble Space Telescope to look for magnesium in Europa's atmosphere, another possible element in Europa's ocean salts. As Lovett summarized:

These observations help us refine our models of Europa's atmosphere, testing what releases sodium and how radiation pressure shapes its distribution. We're also looking for magnesium, which has been tentatively detected on Europa's surface but not yet in its atmosphere. Finding it could provide another important clue to the salts present on this intriguing ocean world.

Further Reading: W.M. Keck Observatory, JGR Space Physics

Biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas lifts the lid on the secret life of tardigrades in stunning detail for the Nikon Small World photography awards.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

It's not often we get to peer into the tiny world of tardigrades (also known as water bears). But through his photography, biologist Gonzalo Quiroga-Artigas is unmasking the secret lives of these creatures in stunning detail.

In one photo, which won Quiroga-Artigas 12th place in Nikon's 2026 Photomicrography Competition, a tardigrade (Hypsibius exemplaris) is seen shedding its tough outer layer, known as a cuticle or an exuvium, while laying an egg in the discarded skin.

"A large part of my research involves imaging, and during the many hours I spend at the confocal microscope, I have come across some incredibly beautiful and unexpected scenes," Quiroga-Artigas, a postdoctoral researcher at the Montpellier Cell Biology Research Center in France, told Live Science in an email.

"An interesting feature of tardigrade reproduction is that some species lay their eggs inside the shed cuticle, or exuvium. The exuvium can therefore provide an additional layer of physical protection for the developing embryos."

In some species, males may place sperm inside the cuticle of a molting female before egg laying, according to National Geographic. In others, the males fertilize the eggs after they have been left inside the cuticle. And some don't even need males to reproduce at all.

"Many species reproduce through parthenogenesis," Quiroga-Artigas said, which is when an embryo develops from an unfertilized egg, also known as a virgin birth. "This means that males are not required for reproduction, and the resulting offspring are genetically very similar to their mothers," he added. The species in the photograph falls into this category.

Molting and egg laying often take place over several hours, but the shedding itself is a relatively fast process. Capturing it on camera is, therefore, no mean feat.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

"Once I had collected animals that were laying eggs, I had to fix, stain, and mount the specimens before imaging them," Quiroga-Artigas said. "I then spent a long microscopy session searching for the right specimen and the right orientation to obtain a high-quality image. Finding a specimen at exactly the right stage of molting, and in an orientation that allows the process to be clearly visualized, is largely a matter of patience and luck."

—Tardigrades survive being dried out thanks to proteins found in no other animals on Earth

—Tardigrades may hitchhike on snails ... and then suffocate in their slime

—'Sexy Mantis,' obscene orangutan and prancing sparrowhawk feature in 2026 Nikon Comedy Wildlife Awards

Photographing these animals is also challenging due to their tiny size. "Working with tardigrades in the lab requires a lot of experience with micromanipulation, as they are extremely small," Quiroga-Artigas said. "Hypsibius exemplaris, for example, is only about 250 µm [micrometers] long." That's about twice the width of a human hair.

This particular photo was taken using confocal microscopy, which uses a focused laser beam to light up one section at a time to create a detailed, high-resolution image. Quiroga-Artigas used this technique for a second tardigrade photo that was listed as an Image of Distinction in the same competition.

The second image submitted by Quiroga-Artigas to the Nikon Small World competition of a tardigrade shown from beneath.

He also received an Honorable Mention in the Nikon Small World in Motion Competition for a video of a pregnant tardigrade making contact with another tardigrade, which can then be seen pooping. However, it's not clear whether the contact between the two individuals caused this movement, Quiroga-Artigas said.

Quiroga-Artigas hopes his photography and videos give viewers an idea of just how beautiful and complex the microscopic world really is. "There are tiny animals all around us that we cannot see with the naked eye, yet they live, reproduce, grow, and undergo complex life cycles just like the animals we are more familiar with," he said.

"I will continue capturing images of tardigrades in different contexts related to my future research, without necessarily having a specific photographic goal in mind," he added. "In my experience, some of the best images I have captured were not necessarily the ones I was actively looking for."

#6452. A Single Fluorescent Dye Can Now Reveal 14 Different Structures Inside Living Cells

Researchers at Peking University have developed a fluorescent dye that can distinguish at least 14 membrane-bound structures in living cells using subtle differences in their chemical environments

Watching the inner workings of living cells has long been difficult because most fluorescent dyes highlight only one cellular structure at a time. Now, researchers at Peking University have developed a dye called JONR that can distinguish at least 14 different structures using a single stain.

The dye changes color depending on the chemical environment surrounding it, allowing scientists to identify cellular structures without labeling each one separately. In laboratory tests, JONR identified organelles with three times the accuracy of Nile red, a fluorescent dye that has been used for more than a century.

JONR is based on Nile red, which glows differently depending on its surroundings. It produces greener light in oily environments and redder light in more polar ones. However, Nile red’s limited color changes make it difficult to tell similar cell membranes apart.

By modifying the dye’s molecular structure, the researchers increased its sensitivity to subtle differences between membranes. JONR also produces very little light in water, reducing unwanted background signals and making cellular structures easier to observe.

Using JONR, scientists were able to track interactions between structures inside living cells. They observed moving compartments called late endosomes pulling thin tubes of the endoplasmic reticulum, a network involved in processing proteins and other cellular activities.

The dye also revealed differences in how tightly molecules are packed within membranes. With specialized microscopy, researchers could examine both membrane composition and molecular organization using the same stain.

Experiments involving nerve cells showed that JONR could detect how molecules are arranged along nerve fibers. Additional tests in migrating cells revealed differences between the membranes of structures involved in cell movement.

The dye showed no significant toxicity in cultured cells, but the research has not yet demonstrated its performance in living animals or humans. Some measurements also require specialized microscopes.

Although further testing is needed, JONR could allow researchers to study several cellular structures and their interactions without relying on multiple fluorescent dyes.

Reference: “Far-red-emitting Nile red with boosted solvatochromism enables multidimensional imaging of membrane heterogeneity and dynamics” by Mingqiao Liu, Yunzhe Fu, Xiaopeng Li, Haolin Zhang, Yumiao Ma, Meiqi Li, Chunyan Shan, Hongxi Zheng, Xiaoyi Lu, Yan Zhang, Li Yu, Peng Xi and Zhixing Chen, 23 February 2026, The Innovation. DOI: 10.1016/j.xinn.2026.101319

Funding: Natural Science Foundation of Shandong Province (Major Basic Research Project), National Key Research and Development Program of China, Beijing Municipal Science and Technology Commission, Beijing National Laboratory for Molecular Sciences, National Natural Science Foundation of China

#6451. This week: Lame duck kicks off with Hegseth impeachment effort

Departing GOP Rep. Thomas Massie of Kentucky told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call file photo) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

The lame-duck session of Congress kicks off this week as the House is expected to consider a resolution to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth while the Senate seeks to advance a bipartisan deal on permitting reform.

Last week’s midterm elections saw Democrats claim sizable majorities in both the House and Senate in the new Congress, and among the immediate questions is whether the demoralized GOP will face attendance woes.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., the expected next speaker of the House, said Sunday that he would support the Hegseth impeachment.

“I'm a hard 'yes' on the Hegseth resolution,” Jeffries said on ABC’s “This Week.” “The so-called secretary of Defense has abused his power, undermined our national security and engineered this reckless and costly war of choice in Iran, which has skyrocketed prices on the American people and made the country less safe. Pete Hegseth has got to go.”

Departing Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., told CQ Roll Call in late October that the Hegseth impeachment resolution would come up in the first week of the post-election lame duck session.

It’s also orientation week on Capitol Hill for new members of Congress. House orientation got underway Sunday.

The Senate, meanwhile, looks to take up a bipartisan permitting bill that has the backing of President Donald Trump.

“This Landmark Permitting Reform Legislation will codify our America First Energy Agenda, and ensure that we can build Pipelines, Mines, and Power Plants faster than ever before, lowering Energy Costs for American Families, and creating High Paying American Jobs,” Trump posted on Truth Social.

Senate negotiators over the weekend released text of an amendment seeking to address remaining concerns.

“I’m grateful for the input throughout this process from Senate and House colleagues, environmental and labor organizations, and Tribal leaders. Our manager’s amendment improves [the bill] and addresses the thoughtful feedback we have received,” Senate Environment and Public Works ranking Democrat Sheldon Whitehouse of Rhode Island said in a statement. “Now it’s time to pass this bill so we can lower costs, juice the clean energy economy, build big things again in America, reduce pollution, and create tons of new well-paying union jobs.”

Beyond the permitting bill, the Senate Republican majority may seek to use its remaining time trying to confirm more of Trump’s nominations before the control of the floor agenda passes to the Democrats.

"We've got the farm bill, the NDAA, and we have that third reconciliation bill that we need to get across the finish line, and there are so many things that we need to get done and buttoned up," including nominations, departing Sen. Marsha Blackburn, R-Tenn., said in a weekend Fox News interview. Blackburn, one of the Republicans who had success at the ballot box, is now governor-elect of Tennessee. But it's an open question how long lawmakers will want to stick around.

There’s also the matter of an imminent fight over funding the government and laying the groundwork for the new Congress. Republican leadership elections are scheduled for Tuesday, while Democratic leadership elections are expected in December. Democratic senators-elect are due on Capitol Hill Monday and Tuesday, according to the office of Senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer, D-N.Y. Schumer is widely expected to be the majority leader in 2027.

There have been some calls for Senate Republicans to delay their elections, though current Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota has been widely expected to remain as the Republican leader.

“One of the things I learned in business and the Army is that after a failure, you have to start with honesty, transparency, and accountability,” Sen. Dave McCormick, R-Pa., said in a Sunday night statement. “As I’ve shared with Leader Thune, I don’t believe we should move to leadership elections until we have digested and debated the lessons of the midterms and how to move forward.”

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., has also been circulating a letter calling for a delay, and he has argued the election should not be held, in part, because the makeup of the Senate Republican Conference is not yet final. Senate races are still not called in Alaska and Mississippi.

Absent this week will be Sen. Christopher S. Murphy, D-Conn., who recently had a stroke.

“The doctors are very encouraged by the progress I’ve made so far. In order to take my recovery seriously and get back to work on the quickest timeline possible, I will be spending several weeks at a rehabilitation center after being discharged from the hospital today,” Murphy said in a Friday statement.

#6450. Making Sense of Chaotic Supernova Ejecta With the JWST

Finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy. But the JWST has the tools to do it. Its Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) and its Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) were built for situations like this.

Massive stars play an important role in the evolution of the cosmos. They're responsible for synthesizing astronomical metals, the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium that are necessary to form everything from rocky planets to living organisms. Without massive stars, the cosmos would look much different. It would be a simple mixture of hydrogen, with a little helium mixed in, and trace amounts of lithium. Nature can't build planets or create life with that limited palette.

Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.

Massive stars live fast and die young, then explode as supernovae. When that happens, the explosion sends their contents, including their astronomical metals, out into the interstellar medium. Once there, it's available not only for planets and life, but for the next generation of stars.

When a supernova explodes, it leaves behind a supernova remnant, the matter ejected by the explosion in an expanding shockwave. The shockwave heats up the expanding shell, creating some of Nature's most stunning displays. The shocks can also rebound, creating an inward shock wave. It can create a real mess, but there are still patterns to be discerned. Within the exanding shell, molecules come form that tell astrophysicists what happened inside the star prior to its explosion.

One of the most well-known supernova remnants is Cassiopeia A (Cas A). It's about 11,000 light years away, and it was observed by Earthlings around 1667. Astronomers are interested in it because they can learn a lot about the exploding star that created itâthe progenitorâby analyzing its contents.

The JWST was built for just such an endeavour. In new research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team of researchers used the JWST's MIRI and MRS to determine Cas A's chemical makeup. The research is "JWST Resolves Dust Emission from Individual Ejecta Clumps in Cassiopeia A: Dominant Grain Compositions Point to a Shell Merger in the Progenitor," and the lead author is Tea Temim, a research scientist from Columbia University.

"We present a study of dust emission in the supernova remnant (SNR) Cassiopeia A (Cas A) observed with the MIRI Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) on board JWST," the authors write. "The unprecedented spatial resolution at mid-IR wavelengths allows us to isolate dust emission from individual arcsecond-scale clumps of supernova (SN) ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM) and identify the dominant dust species in each chemically distinct region."

Massive stars fuse different elements in layers, and that's reflected in the remnants they leave behind when they explode. Increasingly heavier elements are forged in the core, up until iron is reached. Lighter elements are fused together in the surrounding layers. These layers tell the star's history, but it all gets blown into space when the star explodes as a supernovae. To make matters more complicated, these shock waves can bounce back as reverse shocks.

The clumps in the supernova ejecta that the authors refer to are huge, as large as our Solar System. In studying these clumps with the MRS, the researchers were able to identify different dust species region by region, rather than as one mixed up jumble of spectra. They learned that the progenitor star underwent a shell merger.

âMaterial within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,â lead author Temim said in a press release. âSo, for example, this would be something like the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merging together and changing the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.â

Before they turned to the JWST, they used Spitzer images to identify regions to focus on with the JWST.

This figure shows Spitzer images on the left and JWST images on the right. The JWST obviously has a much higher resolution, and the researchers used it to map Cas A's dust chemistry all across the remnant. The observations led to a better understanding of the shell mergers the remnant went through right before it exploded, and a better understanding of the progenitor's overall structure. Since astrophysicists can't see inside stars, they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, JPL-Caltech, T. Temim (Columbia University), R. Arendt (UMBC), D. Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI).

The Spitzer identified regions with different dust properties. The researchers focused on three of them with MRS.

"The MRS spectra extracted at positions P1, P2, and P3 ... all exhibit significant emission from warm dust, but with spectral shapes that differ considerably between the three regions," the authors write.

This image shows the overall supernova remnant and the locations of three regions with distinctly different dust properties first identified with the Spitzer Space Telescope. The researchers examined these regions more closely with the JWST's MRS, seen as P1, P2 and P3. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Danny Milisavljevic (Purdue University), Tea Temim (Princeton University), Ilse De Looze (UGhent); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

P1 samples reverse-shocked ejecta that has bright argon emissions dominate by grains of SiO2 (silica). It helps the researchers track the outer layers of the supernova's ejecta. Finding it supports the idea that the progenitor underwent a carbonâoxygen shell merger.

P2 is centered on what astronomers call Cas A's "Green Monster" structure, which is the green structure near the center. It's emissions are attributed to circumstellar matter emissions on Cas A's near side, not material from Cas A's progenitor. It's likely made of mostly Mg2SiO4, which helps astronomers determine that the progenitor's dust and the CSM dust are distinct from one another.

P3 is another reverse-shocked region. It has very bright neon emissions compared to P1. That favours another shell merger, this time between a carbon shell and an oxygen shell.

This image of Cas A is from the JWST's MIRI F2100W filter. The P1, P2, and P3 regions are indicated by the white arrows. "The spatial distribution of the P2-like emission associated with Mg2SiO4 CSM dust is shown in green, P1-like emission associated with SiO2 dust is shown in magenta, and P3-like Ne-rich emission associated with carbon dust is shown in blue," the authors write. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

"Identifying the different types of dust grains formed in the chemically distinct layers of a supernova brings us one step closer to understanding how much dust supernovae contribute to the interstellar dust reservoir in our galaxy," said co-author Ilse De Looze, associate professor at Ghent University in Belgium. "By revealing the composition of this newly formed supernova dust, JWST also provides crucial insights into how well these grains can survive the powerful reverse shocks that sweep through the supernova debris, ultimately determining how much dust can escape into the interstellar medium."

This JWST image of Cas A has the synchrotron emissions subtracted. Since synchrotron emissions are non-thermal, and since their emission lines overlap the lines from thermal dust, removing them helps to isolate the signal from the ejecta, which is what the researchers are interested in. So this image basically tracks the thermal emissions from carbon dust. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

The JWST played a leading role in this effort to piece together what happened to Cas A's progenitor. But it's observations added to an existing observational base from JAXA's XRISM x-ray satellite and NASA's own Chandra X-ray Observatory. Taken together, the more complete picture shows that the progenitor's shell mergers were underway prior to its explosion as a supernova.

After all the imaging, processing, and fitting to models, this is the overall result. This figure shows which parts of the Cas A ejecta are from the existing circumstellar medium (left: Mg2SiO4 grains) and which parts are actually form the progenitor star (right: SiO2 grains.) Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26

âWith Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,â said Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in the United States. âAs a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. Itâs telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.â

These results will also help build better model for understanding other supernova remnants.

The authors say this work shows how important the JWST's high-resolution images are for understanding dust ejecta in supernova remnants and how it was formed. (But smart Universe Today readers already know how important the JWST is.)

"It also demonstrates that spatially resolved dust compositions in young SNRs can serve as a powerful probe of the chemical structure and explosion properties of core-collapse SNe," they conclude.

Eater Awards celebrated the best restaurants, chefs, and more of 2026

What a night. On Sunday, November 15, the winners of the 2026 Eater Awards, presented by Capital One, celebrated together at Nine Orchard in NYC. More than 200 chefs, restaurateurs, bartenders, and friends of Eater — many of whom traveled across the country to be there — partook in live portraiture, custom engraving, and, of course, plenty of food and drink.

Now in its 17th year, the Eater Awards recognize the year’s best new restaurants, bakeries, bars, dishes, and chefs in markets across the U.S.. More than 30 Eater staffers and contributors spent months traveling to 44 cities to weigh contenders on food, service, atmosphere, and the stories behind them. The prize? A tomato can trophy. And yes, they’re real.

The night started off strong with photos at the tomato can-wrapped step-and-repeat and a welcome shot of Zbiotics, before guests headed up to the roof of Nine Orchard for panoramic views and more fun. The party was filled with unique moments, from custom lighter engraving presented by Toast to live water color portraits presented by Capital One. Rounds of dishes inspired by the winning restaurants were passed.

A champagne toast commemorated the resiliency of the hospitality industry. “Thank you for what you do, every single day, to bolster your team, your community, and the restaurant industry at large,” said Eater editor in chief Stephanie Wu.

Rose Previte of DC’s Maydan, Medina, and Souk, and 2026 Best New Restaurant winner Maydan Market LA joined Wu on stage to present the first-ever Pre Shift Future of Hospitality Award to Maison Bar à Vins. This peer-voted award honors one winner whose work is particularly forward-thinking, challenges conventions, sets new standards, and points toward the future of hospitality. Matt Conroy and Jason Chavenson took home the surprise award.

“It’s really amazing to win an award like this that’s voted by everybody here and, you know, so many people we look up to, so it’s really incredible,” said Matt Conroy.

All attendees received an Eater tote filled with editor-curated products including Bubs candy, Zbiotics, TimeSavvy’s self-care and travel essentials kit, sweet matcha drops and fiery garlic chili sauce from Bokksu, a Wood Cabin candle from Keap Candles, chef socks from Cargo Crew, and a gift certificate for a pair of shoes from Snibbs.

It truly was a great night celebrating the hard work these chefs and their teams put into creating the best dining experiences of the year. Feeling FOMO? Check out the full list of winners and see for yourself what made these restaurants and chefs stand out.

#6448. A Tiny Twist Reveals a Hidden Atomic Grid That Changes How Electricity Behaves

Scientists have discovered that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets creates a hidden grid of atomic defects that alters how electrical charges are distributed.

Twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets together has allowed scientists to create a hidden grid of atomic defects that influences how electrical charges are arranged. The grid forms where the crystals meet, producing tiny patterns of electrical polarization that could eventually help researchers develop new electronic technologies.

The discovery, led by researchers at the Technical University of Denmark (DTU) and published in Nature, demonstrates how the angle between two bonded crystals can control the spacing of defects at their interface. Although practical applications remain uncertain, the technique offers a way to engineer electrical structures at the nanoscale.

The researchers worked with strontium titanate (SrTiO3), a chemically stable oxide widely studied for its electronic properties. They fabricated crystal sheets just 10 nanometers (about 0.0000004 inches) thick and assembled them with a controlled twist.

The underlying principle resembles a moiré pattern, which appears when two regular grids overlap at slightly different angles. However, strong bonding between the crystal sheets caused their atoms to rearrange at the interface. The remaining mismatch became concentrated along narrow regions of crystal distortion called dislocations, forming a repeating square grid.

“We have spent years learning how to make high-quality sheets, put them together in the right position, bond them and twist them. Once you can do all of that, you can start looking at what happens where these two sheets meet,” says Professor Nini Pryds of DTU.

“So, the bonding is essential to understanding what happens between the layers.”

The grid was first predicted by William Sandholt, then a Ph.D. student at DTU, using machine learning simulations to calculate how atoms would rearrange as the crystals bonded and twisted. His results identified a network of dislocations that the researchers subsequently searched for experimentally.

Early electron microscope images showed what appeared to be an ordinary moiré pattern, with no obvious sign of the predicted defects. One difficulty was that the microscope’s electron beam passed through material on both sides of the buried interface, making its atomic structure difficult to isolate.

“The electron beam goes through about ten nanometers of material, reaches the interface, and then goes through another ten nanometers. So, the image is influenced by the material on both sides of what we want to see,” explains John Mangeri, a postdoc at DTU and joint first author of the study.

To overcome this problem, the team simulated how electrons traveled through the samples and examined thin cross sections cut in different directions. Electron microscopy performed with collaborators at the University of Antwerp in Belgium and the SuperSTEM Laboratory in the UK ultimately confirmed the predicted grid.

“Right where the sheets met, we could see the repeating pattern, and it agreed almost perfectly with the theory. That was amazing.”

Pryds emphasizes that the theoretical predictions were essential to the discovery.

“We would never have discovered the dislocations if the calculations had not predicted their existence. The finding highlights the power of combining theory and experiment, bringing together researchers who synthesized the ultrathin sheets, assembled them with a controlled twist, simulated their behavior, and examined the resulting material.”

Further simulations showed that the atomic distortions surrounding the dislocations could slightly separate positive and negative electrical charges. This separation, known as polarization, formed swirling patterns around the grid. Additional microscopy, interpreted alongside the simulations, supported the connection between the atomic distortions and these electrical structures.

The spacing of the grid also depends on the angle between the crystal sheets, providing a means of adjusting the size of the resulting patterns.

“Changing the twist angle changes the spacing between the dislocations. So now, we have a way to control how small the structure becomes,” says joint first author William Sandholt.

“These dislocations could be used for memory applications, for example, and the grid could be tuned through the twist angle.”

Electrical polarization plays a role in technologies such as memory devices and energy storage systems, making these structures potential candidates for future research. The team plans to investigate whether the same approach can produce useful electrical behavior in strontium titanate or other oxides.

Reference: “Designing dislocation-driven polar vortex networks in twisted perovskites” by W. Sandholt, N. Gauquelin, J. Mangeri, A. Annys, J. M. Hansen, A. R. Insinga, E. Dollekamp, N. Vitaliti, G. Panchal, T. Chennit, A. De Backer, D. Kepaptsoglou, R. Mandal, D. R. Rodrigues, S. Van Aert, H. Nguyen, K. I. Wurster, A. Bhowmik, I. E. Castelli, S. B. Simonsen, T. S. Jespersen, Q. M. Ramasse, R. D. James, B. Jalan, J. Verbeeck, J. M. G. Lastra and N. Pryds, 18 November 2026, Nature. DOI: 10.1038/s41586-026-11330-9

This work was supported by the European Research Council (ERC) Advanced Grant NEXUS and the Villum Investigator Grant EUREKA.

Scientists have discovered that twisting two ultrathin crystal sheets creates a hidden grid of atomic defects that alters how electrical charges are distributed. VERY GOOD.

Scientists should think deeply: Is distortion a change in spatial structure? Can changes in spatial structure alter the physical properties of matter? Why?

The study on bilayer twisted strontium titanate (SrTiO3) crystals, published in Nature, is regarded by the mainstream academic establishment as a major leap forward in nanoelectronics. However, if we strip away its intricate experimental veneer and examine it through the lenses of FAST (Fluidized Absolute Space Theory) and TVT (Topological Vortex Theory), it is precisely a brilliant manifestation of “geometric reality” within macroscopic matter.

Mainstream physics tends to shroud such phenomena in the fog of complex quantum field theory and energy band calculations. Yet, by returning to nature and geometric intuition, we discover that this is actually an ideal physical sandbox for the “medium-structure” dualistic model in TVT.

On the surface, this Nature report appears to be a materials science breakthrough regarding novel memory devices; however, under the lenses of FAST and TVT, it is a vivid experimental report on “how topological defects shape physical reality.” It inadvertently demonstrates that whether it is the curvature of spacetime in the vast universe or charge polarization at the nanoscale, their underlying logic is interconnected—all things originate from geometry, and the ultimate truth of physics is hidden within the topological structures of those vortices and grids.

The return of science ultimately requires breaking through the red tape of the academic establishment to reclaim a sense of awe and intuition for nature and geometry.

Is twisting two ultrathin crystal a change in spatial structure?

When a crystalline lattice is ordered and aligned cleanly, it behaves as a low-resistance conduit rather than throwing up heavy impedance barriers against incoming light or charge.

In standard solid-state physics, people describe this through periodic band structures, coherent wave propagation, or low scattering along symmetric crystal axes. Looking at this through a continuous-medium lens, an aligned crystalline structure provides a continuous, harmonious coupling path: when a wave or charge enters along a well-matched structural channel, temporal gradient impedance (∇ZT) stays low along that path, rotational closure (Ωπ) matches the local geometry smoothly, and propagation approaches an open-conduit regime (ΔZ → 0) instead of shedding energy at abrupt mismatches.

What makes a twisted-layer crystal grid so interesting alongside that conduit behavior is what happens when you introduce a controlled twist between layers: instead of a uniform, uninterrupted channel everywhere, the twist creates localized regions of strain and structural reorganization where impedance and coupling are concentrated, while the surrounding ordered regions still carry their underlying lattice character governed by π.

Applied to an energy distribution architecture in something like a spacecraft heat shield, pairing low-impedance conduit channels with a tunable twist-grid interface offers a practical way , The main reasoning of managing extreme entry loads. Rather than letting intense thermal and electromagnetic stress concentrate at a single hotspot, ordered pathways can guide energy away from high-load zones while localized twist-grid impedance boundaries help shed, disperse, and buffer torsional shear and charge tension across a broader structural network. #6447. A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability

A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given starâs initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

The authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across âspaceâ by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and âtimeâ by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, says Biddle.

Some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, says Biddle. We donât see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

By âstellar misalignment,â Biddle means that the starâs spin axis points in a different direction than the orbital axis of a planet. In contrast, a system is aligned when the starâs equator lies in the same plane as the planetâs orbit, like a spinning top placed at the center of a hula hoop.

It is misaligned when the starâs spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a starâs tilt and the orbitâs tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

Thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

We deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, says Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

This artist's conception shows a binary-star, or two-star, system, called HD 113766, where astronomers suspect a rocky Earth-like planet is forming around one of the stars. At approximately 10 to 16 million years old, astronomers suspect this star is at just the right age for forming rocky planets. The system is located approximately 424 light-years away from Earth. Credit: NASA/R. Hurt, JPL-Caltech/C. Lisse, JHUAPL

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, says Biddle.

A Plethora Of Strangely Mis-Aligned Exoplanets

But prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the Solar System, where planets are mostly aligned with the Sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, says Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

Our own solar systemâs planetary alignments are pretty much coplanar.

The Sunâs spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, says Biddle.

Biddle doesnât know for certain if the Sunâs axis was tilted from the start.

But if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the Sun could have become tilted, says Biddle. They include a past fly-by of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds, and even internal gravity waves, she says.

There isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, says Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.
