#6446. What 8 Cool Food People Outsource for Thanksgiving

﻿Laila Gohar, Deb Perelman, and others share their top tips

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

A few Novembers ago, I had a mild crash out over puff pastry. I was planning to meet my partner’s extended family for the first time over Thanksgiving, and volunteered to bring a holiday staple a few weeks prior (in what was one of the most helpful, albeit intimidating Excel sign-up sheets I’ve ever seen). What could be easier than apple pie? The ingredients for the recipe I found weren’t fussy, and it hardly called for fancy technical skills. Plus, I could make it ahead of time knowing that it would travel well.

Then I remembered the puff pastry. For some reason, I attached a moral imperative to the idea of making the whole pie from scratch, and spent the next two weeks poring over puff pastry recipes that felt like casual guides to wizard-tier alchemy. I loved to cook, but I simply wasn’t a big baker. (I also didn’t own a food processor, unless you counted my Magic Bullet.) My mother eventually brought me down to Earth. “Just buy it,” she told me over the phone, undoubtedly rolling her eyes. “Everyone knows it’s a pain in the butt.” Even the Barefoot Contessa herself, she reminded me, famously avoids the time-consuming task (“Nobody wants to make puff pastry!”).

Those words set me free. Once I realized that I could outsource my puff pastry, and the source of my Thanksgiving stress, I was finally able to relax and enjoy the holiday. Folks take pride in their Turkey Day dishes, as they should, but there’s nothing wrong with accepting a little help.

In the hopes of encouraging you to lighten your load, my colleague Bettina Makalintal and I asked some of the coolest people we know in the food industry what they prefer to outsource for Thanksgiving, from smoked hams to appetizers, in order to keep their holiday stress-free.

“There is a single premade item that I purchase for Thanksgiving: a smallish in-house smoked ham from The Meat Hook. It’s a sort of whatever part of the Thursday meal — I make a banging turkey, which commands most of the attention. But! The ham has become a key player during what my family calls Leftover Sandwich Weekend. Having an extra piece of protein mitigates any concerns about not having enough turkey left over. More importantly, a thin slice or two adds a salty, fatty, sweet, and smoky layer to the sandwich architecture. Much needed, very appreciated. Ham: I can’t imagine a turkey sandwich without it.” — Carla Lalli, cookbook author of books including Food is a Feeling

“I outsource pies because I don’t especially enjoy making them… or eating them!”— Laila Gohar, food-based conceptual designer, artist, and co-founder of Gohar World

“I almost always outsource appetizers and/or a cheese plate. If I’m making the big stuff (turkey, stuffing, sides, desserts… okay, I’m also a control freak with more time to cook than most), I feel absolutely overwhelmed if I am also making small things. So while I have a couple really simple apps I’ll put out if there are no volunteers, I much prefer having a friend or family member bring their favorite wedge of cheese and crackers, or [crossing fingers] bacon-wrapped dates. Here is one of my simple go-tos (it’s also in my Smitten Kitchen Every Day cookbook): herb-and-garlic baked Camembert. I’d still prefer if someone else can prep it; I don’t mind heating it up.” — Deb Perelman, cookbook author and recipe developer behind Smitten Kitchen

“We outsource lumpia from Chuck’s mom. We love having them for the holiday but don’t like frying at home when we have everything else cooking that day. She always has a couple hundred in her freezer ready and waiting to be fried for special occasions.” — Hailee Catalano and Chuck Cruz, cookbook authors and recipe developers behind @2peoplecooking

“I usually get a roast duck from Hay Hay Roasted in Chinatown, because they’ve got it down. It’s consistently delicious and not everyone eats turkey in our family.” — Camari Mick, chef and founder of Calabash

“I always outsource the pre-dinner snacks to the grocery store. I have so much respect for people who can construct elaborate cheese boards or spend the morning filling puff pastries, but that’s just not me. I like to set out a few bowls with tamari almonds, Castelvetrano olives, and — this is the most important one — Nacho Cheese Doritos. They’re the perfect mix of salty, crunchy little snacks to have with a drink before dinner is ready. The Doritos always get cleaned out first, so keep a backup bowl waiting in the kitchen.” — Casey Elsass, columnist at Cup of Jo and author of What Can I Bring?

“Last year for Friendsgiving, we collectively decided to skip the hassle of making the turkey and instead ordered Popeyes’ Cajun-Style Turkey. It’s rubbed with a blend of Louisiana-style Cajun spices and comes fully cooked, so all you have to do is thaw, heat, and serve it. It really set the tone for a very unserious dinner, which I think is what you want at a Friendsgiving. We’ll be ordering it again this year.” — Anna Archibald and Kevin Serai, content creators and recipe developers behind Cabagges.World

“We’re fairly relaxed about Thanksgiving, but if we do end up making food on that day, I usually outsource pie dough! I’m happy to buy organic frozen pie dough because usually it tastes fine and it saves me a little bit of time. I realized I prefer to spend my energy on the other parts of the meal, and I prefer not to add on to my own mental load by also making pie dough. I know it’s quick and easy; I’d just rather not! But I do make my own fillings.” — Ifrah F. Ahmed, author of Soomaaliya

#6445. Earth’s Soil Is Worth $325 Trillion – so Why Is Nobody Protecting It?

Saharan dust helps nourish the Amazon, showing why scientists argue that protecting soil requires countries to look far beyond their own borders.

Nearly everything we eat depends on the thin layer of soil covering Earth’s surface. This vital resource also filters water, stores carbon, and supports ecosystems that sustain life. Yet despite its importance, soil remains without a dedicated international treaty to protect it.

Estimates cited in a study published in the European Journal of Soil Science suggest that up to 40 percent of the world’s land is already degraded, putting US$44 trillion in annual economic output at risk.

Binding international agreements protect the atmosphere, biodiversity, and the high seas. Soil, an estimated US$325 trillion (A$473 trillion) natural asset, receives fragmented protection through agreements on climate change, biodiversity, and desertification.

The United Nations Convention to Combat Desertification focuses on drylands, while other agreements address individual functions such as carbon storage or biodiversity. None provides comprehensive, binding protection for soil as a planetary system.

The paper’s authors, University of Sydney soil scientists Dr. Quentin Styc and Professor Alex McBratney, argue that this gap partly reflects a misunderstanding of the resource itself.

“We have spent centuries classifying soils according to their different properties, uses and locations. But in doing so, we’ve lost sight of the bigger picture,” said lead author Dr. Styc, from the university’s School of Life and Environmental Sciences and Sydney Institute of Agriculture.

Consider the connection between the Sahara Desert and the Amazon rainforest. Each year, around 27.7 million metric tons of Saharan dust cross the Atlantic, delivering roughly 22,000 metric tons of phosphorus to the Amazon. This natural fertilization replaces nutrients lost through flooding, helping sustain one of the world’s most biodiverse ecosystems.

Erosion, pesticide contamination, and microplastics can also spread across borders, while soil degradation can contribute to climate change and food insecurity far from the affected region.

“Soil doesn’t stop functioning at national borders. What happens to soil in one country can have profound consequences for ecosystems, economies and food security on the other side of the world.

“We have international treaties to protect the ocean and atmosphere. Yet the soil beneath our feet, which is fundamental to human civilization, remains without equivalent protection.”

For Styc and McBratney, these links mean soil must be understood and protected as one interconnected global system.

“These connections demonstrate why soil security cannot be achieved by countries acting independently,” Dr. Styc said.

“We need to think about soil in the singular, just as we increasingly talk about one ocean rather than separate oceans. It’s a change in language that reflects a much bigger change in how we understand our responsibility for the planet.”

A proposal for international protection is already taking shape. Aroura, a global soil security think tank established at the University of Sydney, has outlined an eight-stage pathway toward a Global Convention to Secure Soil, targeting adoption in 2032. The proposed convention would coordinate international efforts while allowing countries to develop strategies suited to their environmental and economic circumstances.

In October 2025, the International Union for Conservation of Nature approved a resolution calling for a binding international legal instrument on soil security. Ocean governance offers a model for what cooperation could achieve. After decades of negotiations, an international agreement protecting marine biodiversity beyond national jurisdictions entered into force in January 2026.

“When environmental damage crosses borders, international cooperation needs to match the scale of the problem. We cannot solve a planetary challenge with a patchwork of disconnected policies,” Dr. Styc said.

Aroura brings together an international panel of leading experts in soil science, economics, law, and social science to develop the scientific evidence and policy frameworks needed for a convention. It hosted the Third Global Soil Security Summit at the University of Sydney from October 20 to 23, 2026.

“Soil underpins our food systems, biodiversity, water security and climate resilience, yet it remains largely invisible in international environmental governance,” said co-author Professor McBratney, a leading international soil scientist who was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 2026.

“Through Aroura, we are working to build the scientific and policy foundations for a global convention that recognizes soil as a shared responsibility. We have the knowledge and the tools. What we need now is international commitment.”

Reference: “One Soil, One Planet, No Treaty” by Quentin Styc and Alex McBratney, 3 November 2026, European Journal of Soil Science. DOI: 10.1111/ejss.70448

Funding was received from the Australian Research Council.

Fossil teeth from two caves in southern China are revealing that at least two lineages of early humans were present in the region around 184,000 years ago.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Homo erectus was adaptable enough to live in rainforests in what is now southern China and may have lived alongside Denisovans there, two new studies hint.

The research is based on the incredibly rare findings of nine fossil teeth from ancient humans — eight from H. erectus and one from a mystery human in the genus Homo. The teeth reveal that H. erectus lived in China much more recently than previously thought and that this population likely devoured tropical food found there.

"I think it's exciting because it means that there are two hominin populations occupying these rainforest conditions there at the same time," study first author Frido Welker, a molecular palaeoanthropologist at the University of Copenhagen in Denmark, told Live Science.

H. erectus is generally seen as the first human species to venture out of Africa, after evolving about 2 million years ago. It spread through eastern Eurasia, reaching China and Indonesia between about 1.6 million and 1.8 million years ago. It is one of the longest-surviving hominin species, and the last known record of it is from 108,000 years ago in river flood plains in Java, Indonesia. However, there was no physical evidence of H. erectus being on the Asian mainland more recently than 400,000 years ago.

But in two caves in Guangxi province in southern China, researchers have found thousands of mammalian fossils, accumulated there by porcupines that scavenged for and collected bones. The Baxian and Naxian caves are about 9 miles (15 kilometers) apart, sitting in a karst landscape of limestone formations that are prone to dissolving to create caves that would have offered crucial shelter for H. erectus.

The entrance to Naxian Cave, as seen by a drone, is the tall and wide opening of a cave that goes back around 330 feet (100 meters) to a fossil chamber.

Researchers found the nine human teeth among more than 18,000 fossils, including from apes, elephants, rhinoceroses and other ancient hoofed animals, Welker and his colleagues reported in a study published Wednesday (Nov. 18) in the journal Nature.

Radiometric dating of the fossils and surrounding sediments by methods including assessing the decay of uranium, pins them to about 324,000 to 184,000 years ago. Eight of the teeth have physical features reminiscent of H. erectus, but the ninth is more elusive. It looks distinct from H. erectus, Neanderthals and modern humans, Welker said.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

Welker's team took samples from five teeth ‪—‬ four from the group that seemed to be H. erectus and one from the mysterious tooth ‪—‬ to see which ancient proteins were present, since DNA tends to degrade more easily than the proteins in an organism. (The study of these proteins is known as proteomics.)

The four similar ones had protein signatures that matched what had been seen before in H. erectus.

"The morphology is nicely confirmed by the proteomics," Welker told Live Science. Three of these teeth were from males, and the other was from a female, which the team was able to determine based on the presence or absence of amelogenin-Y, a protein coded for only by the Y chromosome.

Researchers investigating two caves in China have found nine human teeth, eight of which have been confidently identified as belonging to Homo erectus.

However, some parts of the protein signatures differed from what had been seen in other H. erectus remains in China, so the new specimens may be from a previously unknown H. erectus population that perhaps had a slightly different genetic makeup, Welker said.

The finding that H. erectus was present in mainland Asia until at least 184,000 years ago — rather than 400,000 years ago — fills a geographical and chronological gap, helping to explain how H. erectus was on Java 108,000 years ago.

"This brings the history of H. erectus in East Asia closer in age to the late Javanese examples, raising the possibility that these populations were connected through land bridges at times of lowered sea level," Chris Stringer, a paleoanthropologist at the Natural History Museum in London who was not involved in the research, told Live Science in an email.

John Hawks, an anthropologist at the University of Wisconsin-Madison who wasn't involved in the study, previously believed that specimens from the past 400,000 years or so flagged as H. erectus were actually Denisovans ‪—‬ ancient humans who lived in Asia, disappeared around 30,000 years ago and belonged to the Homo longi lineage. But he told Live Science that the new morphological and protein findings provide convincing evidence that H. erectus did survive until relatively recently in some places.

The fifth analyzed tooth, known as PA1796, remains mysterious. The protein analysis revealed it was from a male, but it didn't show a recognizable signature in the protein sequence data. Therefore, Welker's team suggested it could be from another hominin species that was present in the region at the same time.

Welker didn’t want to speculate about which species it might be, but said: "Sequence-wise it doesn't have this Homo erectus substitution and morphologically, it doesn't look like an erectus tooth."

The tooth could be from a previously unknown human species, but many experts suspect it is from a Denisovan.

"With some of the new material probably dating to less than 200,000 years old, this already brings it close in age to known or putative Homo longi/Denisovan samples in southern China and Laos, implying potentially long overlaps between these species," Stringer said. "Tooth PA1796 could represent a longi/Denisovan, though it is relatively small in size, and relevant comparative data for longi/Denisovans is sparse."

The entrance to China's Naxian Cave, which has a small opening and goes back around 164 feet (50 m) to a fossil chamber.

Recent research suggests there was interbreeding between the H. erectus and Denisovan lineages, and the new evidence increases the likelihood that this happened, at least occasionally, Stringer said.

Any firm conclusions of who the tooth is from will have to wait for further finds of similar teeth elsewhere, Welker said.

Hawks agreed that the tooth is most likely from a Denisovan, perhaps from a divergent branch for which we don't have protein data. But it could also be from a novel H. erectus population or someone from the same population as the other teeth who, for developmental or genetic reasons, wasn't typical. "I would have liked to see additional comparisons in the paper to more Denisovan teeth," Hawks said.

In another paper, also published Nov. 18 in the journal Nature, Kira Westaway, a geochronologist at Macquarie University in Sydney, and her colleagues examined trace elements in the same teeth, as well as in animal teeth from the caves, to see what they revealed about the hominins' diet and local habitat.

Their analysis indicated that this H. erectus population found plants and animals to eat in tropical, rainforest-like ecosystems. Previously, it was thought that only our own species, Homo sapiens, was able to adapt to this type of environment.

"Rather than being confined to open woodland and grassland environments, H. erectus was considerably more ecologically adaptable than many of us have assumed," Stringer said.

"Being adaptable and being flexible are not traits that we associate with ancient human species — these are traits that we associate with H. sapiens," Westaway told Live Science. "Suddenly we're seeing H. erectus being able to survive in environments that we didn't think they could possibly survive in."

And given the mysterious tooth, it is possible that two different early human populations were this adaptable, said Welker, who was a co-author of the study.

A view from Naxian Cave in China, where Homo erectus teeth were found.

Westaway and her colleagues also looked at levels of the element strontium in the teeth, which can shed light on where someone grew up based on the unique strontium levels in water and foods they consumed as children. The team matched these strontium levels to another karst landscape about 200 miles (320 km) away, in the Red River valley of northern Vietnam.

"It looks like H. erectus moved across large areas, traversing this karst landscape in the rainforests" ‪—‬ a finding that adds to our understanding of these ancient humans, Westaway said.

It's absurd that people often think of H. erectus as an unsuccessful species, she added. "We think they were the first to leave Africa, the first to use fire. It blows my mind because they survived six times longer than H. sapiens has survived so far, so I don't see them as unsuccessful."

Hawks' big question, however, is linked to modern humans, who were in the Chinese region from at least 45,000 years ago.

"Denisovan DNA is present in the peoples of Island Southeast Asia, so, modern humans must have run into Denisovans at some point," he said. "If H. erectus was enduring in the same area at the same time, might H. sapiens also have encountered late H. erectus?"

#6443. Space Lasers Are Fast, But Clouds Still Rule the Forecast

Since the launch of Sputnik, humanity has talked to its spacecraft through radio waves. Radio is great for communication through any weather, but it has hit a limit â traditional radio frequencies are highly regulated by bodies like the International Telecommunications Union, which limits the scalability of radio communications networks to meet the growing demand of bandwidth to and from space. The obvious solution is to switch to infrared lasers, which have an extremely high data transfer rate. However, according to a paper available in pre-print on arXiv from Dr. Slava Turyshev â best known to UT readers for his work on turning the Sunâs gravity into a giant telescope â the raw speed of laser communication isnât the bottleneck, itâs the systemâs reliability.

First, letâs take a second to appreciate the leaps and bounds researchers have made passing data over space laser links recently. Perhaps the most impressive mission was a NASA demonstration called TBIRD, which beamed an astonishing 200 gigabits per second (Gb/s) from orbit, and completed a data transfer of five terabytes in a single five-minute pass over its receiving telescope. That is an astonishing speed for laser communication, but it had the advantage of near-perfect conditions.

Those conditions matter for an optical ground station. One challenge is tracking. A radio communications link spreads its signal over a patch hundreds of kilometers wide, whereas a laser from low Earth orbit might illuminate a patch less than twenty meters across. As a spacecraft hurtles overhead at more than seven kilometers per second, keeping a beam thousands of times narrower locked onto a receiving telescope is far harder than hitting a radio dish.

Fraser takes a question about space-based laser communication.

Another obstacle that radio frequency signals donât have to worry about is airplane interference. Ground stations must automatically shut off their uplink lasers if an airplane passes overhead, so as not to blind the pilots (or the planeâs sensors) with a highly concentrated light beam. While each plane overflight is relatively brief, it can cause consistent disruption which isnât a problem for radio communications frameworks.

The real challenge though is the atmosphere. Anyone that looks up at the sky on a cloudless night can see the stars twinkling. That is caused by swirling pockets of warm and cold air in our atmosphere, and in addition to making the stars seem to dance, it also distorts incoming laser light. To correct for this in optical communication systems, engineers have to use fast-moving deformable mirrors in systems called adaptive optics, or specialized light-sorting microchips. Neither option is cheap.

But the real difficulty in the atmosphere for optical communications is simple to explain â clouds. No laser in the optical or near-infrared range can punch through thick cloud cover. So when an optical base station is covered by thick cloud cover, it is essentially impossible to communicate with, knocking out both uplinks and downlinks unless another suitable base station happens to be available.

Fraser talks about the power of adaptive optics to make the atmosphere "disappear"

According to the paper, pairing stations together does get some improvement. A single one can be expected to be available a little more than 60% of the time, but pairing two together in the American Southwest, for example, can bump that up to around 85%. According to another paper from the German Aerospace Center, setting up a network of eight separate optical stations around Australia and New Zealand drops the chance of an outage to just 0.02%.

However, base stations are expensive. Building eight stations for a single mission is economically infeasible â each station costs roughly two million dollars a year to build, staff, and operate. At that rate, delivering a single terabyte of information to a single mission, if it uses a single station, would cost somewhere between three to four thousand dollars. Scaling that up to eight stations to almost guarantee consistent coverage would mean it would cost $18K to send a single terabyte of data.

The only way that math works is by multiple satellite companies splitting the same ground network. If they could keep the ground stations busy at least half of the time, it could drop the price per terabyte into a reasonable range. To support those efforts, there is a push for standardization already in place.

Fraser answers a question about adpative optics alternatives.

The Civil Standard (CCSDS 141.0-B / âO3Kâ) developed by the Consultative Committee for Space Data Systems defines hardware and handshaking specs for high-rate near-Earth links. To support that standard, the US Department of Defense also decided to get involved, introducing the US Space Development Agencyâs Optical Communications Terminal Standard, requiring interoperability across terminals no matter the supplier, which includes requirements for CCSDS communication protocols.

All that being said, according to Dr. Turyshevâs paper, there is very little likelihood that purely optical communication will supplant radio for space communication anytime soon. A better approach would be to offer a hybrid partnership between the two protocols. Lasers can serve as the âheavy-liftâ workhorses, downloading massive videos or Earth-observation imagery, and radio waves can maintain unbreakable lifeline support for steering or handling emergencies. That combined approach offers the best way to make sure astronauts and all of our critical space infrastructure stay connected, no matter the weather down here on Earth.

S. G. Turyshev - Optical Ground Stations for Space Communications:Systems Engineering, Availability, and Service Economics Through 2030

When not writing or engineering things he can be found entertaining his four children, four cats, and two dogs, or running in circles and throwing plastic discs at people to stay in shape.

#6442. ‘Political malpractice’: Calls grow to delay Senate GOP leadership elections

Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., walks through the Ohio Clock Corridor this summer. Now he’s pushing to delay leadership elections for his conference, urging a discussion of last week’s larger than expected losses. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

After last week’s midterm elections saw them lose at least seven Senate seats and the majority, some Republicans are pushing for a reckoning, saying the conference should stop and think about its future.

“After the stunning defeat [we] just can’t continue on business as usual. That kind of defeat demands change,” Sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., said on Monday evening.

Asked if he himself would want to run for Senate minority leader, the Wisconsin Republican responded with a question of his own: “That’s part of our problem. Who’d want the job? Would you want it?”

Though no hopeful had emerged as of Monday afternoon — at least publicly — to challenge current Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., for the top GOP post, the frustration was palpable as Republican senators returned to D.C. and grappled with the election results. Calls grew throughout the day to delay the conference’s leadership elections planned for Tuesday morning.

“Well, I mean, I’m open to hearing what the arguments are for that,” Thune told reporters Monday when asked about the possibility of postponing the leadership votes. “I don’t know if that solves anything, but like I said, it’s going to be a decision that’s ultimately made by Republican senators. We’ll hear them out.”

Johnson told reporters on Monday that if the election is held, he would “leave the room” and walk out. Either way, he seemed certain to at least get a “fulsome” discussion of the topic, as he requested in a letter he sent to Republican Conference Chair Tom Cotton, R-Ark. Four other Republican senators signed on to the letter, hitting the threshold to call a conference meeting under internal GOP rules.

Also signed by Sens. Mike Lee of Utah, Ted Budd of North Carolina, Rick Scott of Florida, and John Kennedy of Louisiana, the letter obtained by CQ Roll Call cites last week’s “stunning defeat” and reads in part: “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice.”

Kennedy said Monday evening that he was asking to postpone the leadership elections because “we need time to talk to each other.”

“We’re like a shop owner who’s losing his customers. It’s not the customer’s job to fix that. It’s the shop owner’s job, and I’m not looking for blame-shifting. I’m looking for self-examination,” he said, adding that he wouldn’t consider running for minority leader himself.

In the letter, the group asked that at the time the leadership elections were set to begin, 9 a.m. on Tuesday, they instead “have a fulsome conference discussion and delay holding leadership elections until we all have a chance to hear from leadership candidates as to what type of collaborative conference governing model we should adopt and what our strategy will be to counter the emboldened Democrats.”

Thune echoed that wording Monday as he spoke to reporters, saying, “I do think that we need to have a very fulsome, robust conversation about where we go from here, and then we’ll see what the consensus of the conference is.”

But Sen. Shelley Moore Capito, R-W.Va., who serves as chair of the Senate Republican Policy Committee, said she has seen such requests launched in the past and didn’t think it would do much to affect the ultimate outcome. “I think Sen. Thune will be reelected,” she said.

And several Senate GOP aides said that they suspected a “robust” conversation wouldn’t do much to delay the plans and that leadership elections were still expected to take place Tuesday. They noted similar efforts from some of those same senators in previous years to sow discord in the ranks.

That includes Scott, who unsuccessfully challenged Thune in 2024 and then-GOP leader Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., in 2022. But Scott told Fox News over the weekend, “I don’t want to run again. I’ve run twice.”

Republicans “failed. We had a horrible night,” Scott said. “Instead of having an [leadership] election, the first thing you do is you say, ‘OK, what are we going to change? We have to change something.’”

Lee floated the idea of waiting until after the uncalled Senate races in Mississippi and Alaska are officially resolved.

An online pressure campaign was building in some of the same MAGA corners of the internet that have pushed to pass a sweeping voter ID bill, known as the SAVE America Act, that has stalled in the Senate. On Monday morning, influencer Scott Presler in an X post urged constituents to call their senators while praising the lawmakers who have already pushed for the leadership elections to be postponed. “Where is everyone else?” he wrote.

Sens. Jim Banks of Indiana and Dave McCormick of Pennsylvania also called for a delay, though they did not appear on Johnson’s letter.

“A week ago, we had the worst election results in decades,” McCormick said in a post on X, calling Tuesday “too soon” to vote for leaders. “I know it’s been practice to go straight to leadership elections in recent years, but we should not rush it.”

Banks similarly said Tuesday was “too soon,” posting on social media, “Our conference needs to sit down and have a frank conversation about where we fell short, what we stand for, and what we’re going to do for the working families who sent us here.”

One senator speaking out in Thune’s defense was Sen. John Cornyn, R-Texas, who competed with Thune for the top spot in 2024 but on Monday said the leader isn’t to blame for the midterm results.

“I think the president needs to look in the mirror and look at the flawed candidates that he endorsed, and the kind of environment that we’re in,” said Cornyn, who is still smarting from losing his primary to a challenger backed by President Donald Trump.

Cornyn’s loss means he has no say in the coming conference leadership elections. But he said, “I think Thune’s a good man, and did as well as he could against a president and an environment that was pretty hostile.”

Not all deals are created equal — but it’s worth scoring cult-fave ceramics, cool-LA-person food gifts, and more

We’re a far cry from the Black Friday traditions of yore. Instead of storming the gates of department stores at dawn for Salad Shooters and Cabbage Patch dolls, we now sit on our own couches to peruse the deals online — and there are lots of deals. Too many deals! But, not enough that are worthy to qualify as truly worthwhile Black Friday promotions. (Ten or 15 percent? Please.) For the most part, however, the digital age of Black Friday deal-hunting is about machete-chopping your way through the roughage of “meh” promotions.

There are exceptions: Black Friday is usually when brands who rarely run promotions release limited-time deals, and it’s the smartest time of year to buy countertop appliances and electronics. Our online-shopping experts have done the hunting for you.

Below, we’ve rounded up the best Black Friday kitchen and food deals that have already gone live, and which are actually worth your time. There are appliances you’ll use daily, dinnerware beloved by the Eater staff’s favorite restaurants, and GOATed French knives. Find the caffeinated beverage of your choice, and let’s shop.

This is the moment to invest anything you’ve ever pined over from heritage cookware brands, including the big kahuna: Le Creuset. Le Creuset’s Dutch ovens and baking dishes are going to be on escalating promotions across various retailers, so snag the colorways you love most while they’re still available.

Oft-imitated but never equaled, KitchenAid’s stand mixers last decades and look damn good on a counter, with their streamlined mid-century design and array of shades. Black Friday is the time to make the splurge, as they’re on sale across Crate & Barrel, Williams Sonoma, Amazon, and other retailers. This porcelain-white 5-quart option is a classic iteration that will look good in every kitchen, and it’s currently 30 percent off.

Renowned for their intricate craftsmanship and ergonomic, lightweight design, Laguiole knives have been made in the same eponymous French village for hundreds of years. The discounts have already started rolling out; there’s a set of six wood-handled knives on sale at Wayfair, a carving set priced down at Overstock that’ll come in handy for serving meat at future holidays, and a cream-colored set on sale at Mark and Graham that comes with the option of custom engraving.

Los Angeles-based lifestyle brand Flamingo Estate is a major fave among Eater editors, ogled for luxe items like its beloved heirloom-tomato-scented candle and Hachiya persimmon vinegar. It’s having a rare sitewide sale this week, with 20 percent off everything, including the new Big Pasta Dinner set and Affogato set with vanilla olive oil and espresso salt. Truly a one-stop-shop for fancy food gifts.

My Eater colleague Bettina Makalintal got me into Jono Pandolfi a few years ago, and the small rose-colored plates I bought with her at their holiday sale have become my favorites for plating desserts. I’m not alone: The New Jersey-based ceramic studio has an impressive roster of restaurants that use its dinnerware, including Gramercy Tavern, Lilia, and restaurants at cool hotels like the Ojai Valley Inn; that’s probably because they’re durable, come in unique colorways, and dishwasher- and microwave-safe. These gems don’t go on sale often, so add them to your cart while you can.

#6440. NASA’s Voyager 1 Just Made History One Light-Day From Earth

NASA’s Voyager 1 has made history after 49 years in space, reaching an astonishing 16.1 billion miles from Earth, where even light takes 24 hours to bring its signals home.

NASA’s Voyager 1 has reached a remarkable new milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to travel one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years in space, humanity’s most distant spacecraft is now so far away that even light takes a full 24 hours to reach it.

A light-day is the distance light travels in one day, approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers). Voyager 1 officially reached that distance at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST) on November 18.

The extraordinary distance means that communicating with the spacecraft now requires immense patience. Scientists at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a radio signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone. Although the signal traveled at the speed of light, it still needed an entire day to cross the enormous distance separating the probe from Earth.

“Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets,” said Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. “But it went on to become central to NASA’s fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.”

Because distances in space are so enormous, astronomers often measure them using the time it takes light to travel between locations. In a vacuum, light moves at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second, making it the fastest known way for information to travel.

Consider a beam of sunlight passing Earth. It would reach the Moon in approximately 1.3 seconds and take about four hours to arrive at Neptune. From Neptune, that same beam would need another 20 hours to reach Voyager 1.

For an even larger comparison, a light-year, the distance light travels over an entire year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Despite the historic achievement, Voyager 1 is currently experiencing a technical problem. NASA engineers have not received science or engineering data from the spacecraft since November 14. However, the probe continues to transmit a carrier signal, the radio signal normally used to send that information back to Earth. By detecting this signal and combining it with calculations of Voyager 1’s trajectory, engineers were able to verify that the spacecraft had reached the one light-day mark. They are continuing to investigate why the expected data are not arriving.

Voyager 1 and its companion, Voyager 2, began their extraordinary journeys in 1977. NASA launched the twin spacecraft during a rare alignment of the outer planets that made it possible to explore multiple worlds on a single mission.

Operated by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these planets, revealing extraordinary new details about the giant worlds and their moons.

Voyager 2 continued farther along its unique route, becoming the first spacecraft to closely examine Uranus and Neptune, the two distant planets known as ice giants. Today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them the only human spacecraft to have ventured beyond the Sun’s protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring magnetic fields and other conditions influenced by the Sun at extraordinary distances.

“Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery,” said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. “Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward new frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.”

The spacecraft are carrying more than instruments designed to explore the cosmos. Each Voyager also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. The records were created as messages for any advanced civilization that might encounter the probes in the distant future.

“Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward,” said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. “Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.”

Voyager 1 is currently traveling at roughly 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, the enormous region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

This protective region helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, an environment that scientists had never directly explored with a spacecraft before Voyager 1 arrived. Voyager 2 crossed the same boundary in 2018, following a different path.

Although both spacecraft are now beyond the heliosphere, the Sun’s effects extend much farther than scientists once understood. By measuring conditions in this distant environment, the Voyagers are helping researchers investigate how far the Sun’s influence extends into the space between stars.

“The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere,” said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. “One big surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun’s influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.”

Maintaining spacecraft that have operated for nearly half a century presents enormous engineering challenges. Over the years, the Voyager team has developed inventive solutions to problems involving aging components, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer.

One of the greatest challenges is the spacecraft’s steadily shrinking supply of electrical power.

Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by shutting down three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing their functions with three alternatives that require less energy. This approach is helping the spacecraft conserve its remaining power and extend the useful life of its nearly 50-year-old radioisotope thermal generator.

The generator works much like a nuclear battery. Rather than relying on sunlight, which is extremely weak at Voyager’s distance, it produces electricity using heat released as plutonium undergoes radioactive decay.

As that process continues, the amount of available electrical power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately 4 watts of power each year, forcing engineers to make increasingly careful decisions about which systems can remain active.

NASA expects the latest power conservation measures to allow both probes to operate their current collections of scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when they will celebrate the 50th anniversaries of their launches.

Even after nearly five decades, NASA maintains regular contact with Voyager 1. Communication is handled by the agency’s Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of powerful radio antennas at three facilities that supports missions exploring the Moon and more distant regions of space.

The immense separation between Earth and Voyager 1 now makes even a simple exchange of messages a lengthy process. A command sent from Earth requires approximately 24 hours to reach the spacecraft. If Voyager 1 immediately sends a response, that signal takes another 24 hours to return.

In other words, a complete exchange of signals now requires about 48 hours, even though those signals travel at the speed of light.

“We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to,” said Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. “Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity’s silent ambassador to the stars.”

#6439. UK-Built X-Ray Telescope Ready For Action at Mercury

A first of its kind instrument shows its stuff prior to arrival at Mercury.

The joint ESA/JAXA BepiColombo mission has arrived at Mercury, and among its arsenal of detectors ready to explore the innermost world is an innovative new instrument.

A University of Leicester team recently released an image of an iconic deep-sky object as a proof of concept test for their Mercury Imaging X-ray Spectrometer (MIXS). Located on the Mercury Planetary Orbiter segment of the BepiColombo spacecraft stack, UK-built MIXS is the first x-ray instrument on an interplanetary spacecraft, and UK Space Agencyâs instrument contribution to the mission.

The image shows the Crab Nebula (Messier 1) in x-ray light. Located 6,500 light-years distant, âThe Crabâ is a prominent x-ray source, located 6,500 light-years distant in the constellation of Taurus the Bull. The Crab Nebula made a fine target for calibration and testing. Itâs rare for an interplanetary mission to deliberately image a deep-sky object, though they do occasionally turn up in star-tracker navigation frames.

MIXS image of the Crab Nebula (inset) overlaid on a visible light background. Credit:ESA/University of Leicester/NASA/GSFC

New Horizons once captured the âWishing Wellâ open cluster NGC 3532 using its LORRI imager.

âX-rays cannot penetrate Earth's atmosphere to the ground so all X-ray telescopes must be in space,â Adam Fox (MIXS Operations Scientist) told Universe Today. âX-rays can only be reflected to a focus at very shallow angles, which means conventional X-ray telescopes must have very long focal lengths (~10 meters) with nested mirrors, meaning a mass of hundreds of kilograms.â

âMIXS uses novel X-ray optics called micro-pore optics which have millions of tiny pores (20 microns wide) to allow an X-ray telescope which is 1 meter in length and weighs only 11 kilograms, making it small and light enough to be flown to Mercury.â

The MIXS instrument had to wait through 8-long years of space travel, until the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) was jettisoned from the stack joined to the Mercury Magnetosphere Orbiter (MMO) and the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) this past September 3rd. This finally exposed MIXS to space, allowing the team an opportunity to calibrate and test the instrument prior to arrival.

The BepiColombo spacecraft stack prior to launch. Credit: ESA

âUntil early September, the Mercury Planetary Orbiter (MPO) which carries MIXS was attached to the Mercury Transfer Module (MTM) which provided power and propulsion during BepiColombo's 8 year cruise to Mercury,â says Fox. âDuring this time, MIXS' view was directly blocked by the transfer module, only following this separation has MIXS had a view of deep space for the first time. MIXS has been switched on periodically during cruise for checkouts of instrument health during which only the behavior of the detectors within could be monitored.â

The image is the result of 55 platform slews over the course of 39 hours on September 11 and 12th shortly after MTM disposal.

MIXS is designed to create a surface map showing the atomic makeup of Mercury at an unprecedented scale. Working in tandem with the Solar Intensity X-ray and particle Spectrometer (SIXS), MIXS will look at fluorescence of surface material created as a result of high energy solar x-rays impacting the surface. MIXS will also document the local environment in x-rays and magnetospheric interaction on the nighttime side of the planet.

The MIXS instrument prior to launch. Credit: University of Leicester.

âThe scientific advantage from having an X-ray telescope at Mercury is that (the) surface emits X-rays when hit by Solar X-rays or particles from the magnetosphere,â Alec McCrea (University of Leicester) told Universe Today. âThese X-rays have characteristic energies corresponding to certain elements which can tell you what the surface is made of. An X-ray telescope can achieve this at a much higher resolution than achieved on previous missions due to both its smaller FOV and imaging capabilities.â

The arrival for the BepiColombo mission at Mercury occurred late last week on November 21st, when Mercury finally captured the attached MMO and MPO pair into an initial elliptical orbit, after a close 635 kilometer pass above the surface of the planet.

This marked a first a âweak stability captureâ for a planetary mission, as BepiColombo moved inside the gravitational influence of Mercury. The thruster fire was also a first for the spacecraft stack post transfer module separation in September.

There was a bit of drama last week as Estrack controllers noted the mission briefly entered safe mode and the planned thruster burn ended prematurely. The spacecraft still achieved 77% of the expected velocity change, enough to enter orbit. BepiColombo is now in a 75 hour orbit around Mercury, versus the original planned 58 hour orbit.

This comes after one Earth, two Venus and six flybys past Mercury needed to enter capture and orbit around the innermost world. The arrival was also extended from December 2025 to this month, due to an issue with the thrusters on the MTM. This is JAXAâs and ESAâs first mission to Mercury, and only the second to orbit the innermost world since NASAâs Messenger mission ended operations on April 30, 2015, becoming the first human-made object to impact Mercury.

The first mission to see Mercury closeup was NASAâs Mariner 10 on 1974.

The timeline for BepiColombo's arrival at Mercury. Credit: ESA

Next comes the release of JAXAâs MMO (Mio) orbiter on December 9-10th, followed by the sun-shield ejection on December 16th. MPO will then settle down into a 480 by 1500 kilometer orbit early next year on March 10th, after which science operations can finally begin on April 6th. BepiColombo is expected to operate around Mercury until the end of the nominal mission in April 2028, with a possible extension until December 2029.

âDevelopment of such instruments is active. For planetary X-ray fluorescence, a MIXS-like instrument is applicable to many airless bodies in the solar system and would be tailored as such,â says Fox. âMicropore optic X-ray telescopes though have since been flown on several astrophysics missions, including SMILE, Einstein Probe and the (Space Variable Objects Monitor) SVOM.â

If youâre up early this week, you can spot Mercury and wave at BepiColombo as well. The planet just passed greatest elongation west of the Sun this past weekend, and sits just below brilliant Venus at dawn.

Itâll be exciting to see what results BepiColombo and MIXS produce as they get down to work in 2027.

#6438. Scientists Shine New Light on One of the Greatest Mysteries in Modern Physics

The search for more efficient power grids could benefit from understanding a hidden rivalry inside copper-based superconductors, where a mysterious quantum state appears to compete with superconductivity.

When researchers used a pulse of light to temporarily suppress superconductivity in a copper-based material, a mysterious quantum state emerged. As superconductivity returned, that state faded. The experiment offers new evidence in a decades-old debate about how certain materials can carry electricity without losing energy.

These materials, known as cuprates, were discovered in 1986, a breakthrough that earned Bednorz and Müller the Nobel Prize in Physics the following year. Their ability to become superconducting at relatively high temperatures has made them especially promising for future technologies, including more efficient power grids, medical equipment, and quantum computers. Yet nearly 40 years later, scientists still do not fully understand what makes their remarkable properties possible.

One of the biggest uncertainties involves the pseudogap, a poorly understood quantum state that appears in cuprates. Scientists have long debated whether it helps superconductivity emerge or competes with it.

“The pseudogap is one of the greatest mysteries in condensed-matter physics. Understanding how it interacts with superconductivity is essential if we want to explain why these materials can carry electricity without energy loss at unusually high temperatures,” says Fabio Boschini, a professor at INRS and specialist in ultrafast spectroscopy of quantum condensed matter.

Boschini, who led the research, holds the Canada Research Chair in Quantum Materials’ Dynamics and is a recipient of an Alfred P. Sloan Research Fellowship.

To investigate the relationship between the two states, his team used a pulse of light to briefly suppress superconductivity and then tracked how the material’s electrons behaved as it recovered. The researchers used time- and angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-ARPES), a technique that allows scientists to observe rapid changes in the electronic properties of materials.

The experiments took place at the INRS Énergie Matériaux Télécommunications Research Centre, using the TR-ARPES endstation at the Advanced Laser Light Source (ALLS).

The measurements revealed electronic states that had remained hidden from conventional techniques. For the first time, researchers directly observed a temporary pseudogap induced by light. When superconductivity was suppressed, the pseudogap emerged in its place. As the material regained its superconducting properties, the pseudogap gradually faded.

“Thanks to the unique capabilities of the TR-ARPES system at the ALLS laboratory at INRS, we were able to directly observe what happens when superconductivity temporarily disappears and then re-emerges. It is a bit like uncovering missing frames from a film that scientists have been trying to piece together for decades,” says Dario Armanno, a PhD student at INRS and first author of the study.

Published in Nature Physics, the findings support the idea that the pseudogap and superconductivity compete rather than cooperate. This challenges the long-standing hypothesis that the pseudogap acts as a precursor, or an earlier state that helps superconductivity develop.

The project also involved international collaborators, including the Center for Computational Quantum Physics at the Flatiron Institute in New York.

“The pseudogap and superconducting states in cuprates are among the most complex phenomena to reproduce theoretically. Our study reveals that they compete with one another and provides new insight into their behavior when both are excited simultaneously,” said Olivier Gingras, Associate Research Scientist at the Flatiron Institute’s Center for Computational Quantum Physics.

Although the work is fundamental research rather than a demonstration of a new technology, a clearer understanding of these competing quantum states could help guide the development of next-generation superconductors and more energy-efficient technologies.

“This research is essential to advancing the quantum technologies of the future. It contributes to the training of highly qualified personnel in a field that is critical to Canada’s technological sovereignty and to the implementation of its National Quantum Strategy,” says François Légaré, Director of the INRS Énergie Matériaux Télécommunications Research Centre.

Reference: “Light-induced asymmetric pseudogap below the critical temperature in cuprates” by D. Armanno, O. Gingras, F. Goto, J.-M. Parent, A. Longa, A. Jabed, B. Frimpong, R. D. Zhong, J. Schneeloch, G. D. Gu, G. Jargot, H. Ibrahim, F. Légaré, B. J. Siwick, N. Gauthier, A. Georges, A. J. Millis and F. Boschini, 20 October 2026, Nature Physics. DOI: 10.1038/s41567-026-03446-6

The work at ALLS was supported by the Canada Foundation for Innovation’s (CFI) Major Science Initiatives Fund. We acknowledge support from the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council of Canada (NSERC), the Canada Research Chairs Program, the Fonds de recherche du Québec – Nature et technologies (FRQNT), the Québec Ministry of Economy, Innovation and Energy, PRIMA Québec, and the Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation’s EPiQS Initiative.

Researchers have zeroed in on a genetic variant in the human brain that came from Neanderthals, and it might protect us from schizophrenia.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A newfound genetic variant inherited from Neanderthals may shrink a part of modern-human brains without having any meaningful effects on mental ability, and it might also reduce the risk of schizophrenia, a new study finds.

"Genetic differences between Neanderthals and modern humans still influence our brains today," study co-author Hugo Zeberg, an evolutionary geneticist at the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology in Germany, told Live Science. Zeberg and his colleague Svante Pääbo detailed their findings Nov. 16 in the journal PNAS.

Before they went extinct around 40,000 years ago, Neanderthals were among the closest relatives of modern humans. More than a decade of research has shown that Neanderthals and modern humans once interbred. Most people not of sub-Saharan ancestry living today possess about 2% Neanderthal ancestry.

Neanderthals' skulls were larger and more elongated than modern humans'. One reason for the differences has to do with the occipital lobe, the smallest of the brain's four lobes, which sits in the back of the skull. The occipital lobe houses the visual cortex, which helps process signals from the eyes. This area was relatively larger in Neanderthals than it is in modern humans.

In the new study, the researchers analyzed modern-human genomes for genetic variants that are related to occipital lobe size and were also likely inherited from Neanderthals. They discovered one such variant associated with the DAAM1 gene, which a 2019 study linked with brain development. This genetic variant was found only in modern humans outside Africa and was seen in five Neanderthal genomes.

Curiously, the Neanderthal variant the scientists detected in modern-human genomes led to an approximately 0.05-cubic-inch (0.85 cubic centimeters) reduction in occipital lobe size per copy of the variant in an individual. This means that the Neanderthal gene was linked to a slightly smaller brain size in modern humans.

A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk.

This effect is the opposite of what experts expected based on Neanderthals' large skull size, Tony Capra, an evolutionary geneticist at the University of California, San Francisco, who was not involved in the research, told Live Science.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

However, it's important to remember that this one gene variant "does not reflect the full set of variations that might have been present in Neanderthals that might have affected the shape and size of their brain structures," Capra noted.

Zeberg and Pääbo also discovered that having two copies of the DAAM1 gene variant was associated with a nearly 10% reduction in the chances of having schizophrenia in modern humans. But there was no apparent link between the variant and intelligence in modern humans.

"A Neanderthal variant can have a relatively strong effect on brain anatomy without affecting intelligence, while also reducing schizophrenia risk," Zeberg said.

Symptoms of schizophrenia can include altered perceptions of reality, such as visual hallucinations and problems with processing visual signals. This makes it "tempting to speculate" that this Neanderthal gene variant's effects on schizophrenia might be associated with the visual cortex. However, there is currently no evidence for such a link, Zeberg said.

Future research along these lines could analyze how other Neanderthal genetic variants influenced modern humans, Capra said, "to see if they had a consistent effect on us." Looking into Neanderthal variants that are missing from modern-human genomes could "show us what makes us modern humans as opposed to them," Capra added.

This article is for informational purposes only and is not meant to offer medical advice.

#6436. Why Mega-Constellations Have a Hidden Space Junk Blind Spot

We are consistently launching more and more stuff into space. As of now, space agencies track more than 30,000 objects larger than a softball, with an expected one million more bullet-sized pieces of debris orbiting Earth that are too small to spot from the ground.. Government agencies and private commercial entities are planning to have up to 100,000 active spacecraft in orbit by the early 2030s, turning some orbital shells into crowded highways. And according to a new paper, available in preprint on arXiv by Federico Toson, a researcher at the University of Padova in Italy, the math that regulatory agencies use to determine whether a satellite is âsafeâ in these highly congested spaces is fundamentally flawed.

To understand why, letâs look at how engineers currently grade collision risk. Standards set by NASA and the European Space Agency rely on color-coded charts that sort missions into one of several buckets based on their risk profile. Categories like âLow,â âMedium,â and âHighâ are self-explanatory, but they eliminate important distinctions in risk profiles, and only look at one satellite at a time. And, crucially, they focus solely on the risk to the company that launched them.

If a company funnels all of its resources into a billion-dollar weather satellite and that satellite is destroyed, that is a financial catastrophe for that one specific company. But if a mega-constellation operator builds thousands of identical satellites at a cost of a million dollars a pop, losing one barely registers on their financial statements. Consequently, according to the risk profile, all relatively inexpensive, reproducible satellites that make up the mega-constellations end up with a âLowâ risk profile.

Fraser talks about how we make sure satellites don't crash into each other.

The algorithm described in the paper exposes the flaw in that logic by separating the risk into two different scores. First is the âIndividual Riskâ â i.e. the traditional metric of the financial hit a satelliteâs owner takes if the spacecraft is destroyed by collision. The second is the âCollective Riskâ, which ignores the cost of each individual satellite, but captures the physical danger each imposes on every other operational satellite in its altitude band across its entire operational and disposal lifetime.

Mathematically, this is a way of capturing the âtragedy of the commonsâ aspect of orbital space. Economists have long warned that when a âpublic goodâ (such as an orbital path) is free to use, users, whether they are farmers on a field or launch companies trying to build internet satellite constellations, have an incentive to utilize as much of the free resource as they can while not paying any attention to the consequences of that use.

In orbit, those consequences take the form of congestion, dodging maneuvers, and potential destruction of other satellites that are forced on every other company if one decides to ignore their responsibility to properly manage the impact their equipment has on an orbit. As weâve reported before, those consequences are growing, with an average Starlink satellite having to fire its thruster at least once a week to dodge a potential collision.

Fraser talks about how space junk could eventually block our access to orbit.

Starlink itself is a good case in point. A single Starlink V2 Mini, orbiting at 525 km, has a collective risk 317 times higher than the âindividual risk.â In a traditional risk assessment, this would mark it as âLowâ risk, whereas this new framework would place it very clearly in the âVery Highâ camp.

There have been some efforts to capture this long-term environmental impact already. ESA uses an index called the Environmental Consequences of Orbital Breakups (ECOB) and researchers at EPFL in Switzerland have put forward the Space Sustainability Rating. However, the simulations underpinning these metrics are computationally expensive and require hours to complete. The tool Toson developed in MATLAB runs in seconds on a standard computer and matches the higher-end benchmarks exceptionally well.

Itâs all good to simply update the categorization of a satellite for its collective risk, but having that information is useless if operators and regulators donât do anything with it. Toson suggests updating the international debris guidelines and licensing rules to take this new metric into account. If a company wants to launch a low-cost satellite that will affect the orbital environment for everyone else, they should be required to either fund active debris cleanup or accept a cap on the total risk posed by their fleet of spacecraft.

Fraser talks about real-life advanced tech that can remove space debris.

Regulators havenât had much time to digest this new idea, so donât expect to see any such rules anytime soon. But as our orbital highways become more and more congested, satellite operators will need more guidance on how to maintain the commons before we end up in a Kessler Syndrome situation. This new paper may contribute to that standards-setting â and the sooner the better.

F. Toson - A simplified engineering algorithm for collision risk assessment and classification of LEO satellites

UT - Solving the Space Junk Crisis Isn't Just About Counting TrashâItâs About Control and Economics

UT - Are Mega-Constellations Sleepwalking Low Earth Orbit into Runaway Chaos?

#6435. Two Overlooked “Forever Chemicals” Linked To More Than Double the Risk of Liver Cancer

Two little-studied “forever chemicals” have been linked to substantially higher odds of liver cancer in a new University of Southern California (USC) study. People with the highest blood concentrations of either chemical had roughly two to two-and-a-half times the odds of developing the disease compared with those with the lowest concentrations.

The association was especially strong among people genetically predisposed to fatty liver disease. Published in Environmental Health Perspectives, the findings suggest that inherited susceptibility may influence how environmental chemical exposures affect cancer risk.

Researchers analyzed blood samples from 223 people who later developed hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC), the most common form of liver cancer, and 223 matched controls. The samples were collected an average of 7.8 years before diagnosis as part of the Multiethnic Cohort Study (MEC), which has tracked more than 215,000 participants in California and Hawaii since the 1990s.

Of the 12 per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) measured, two showed significant associations with liver cancer: perfluoroheptanoic acid (PFHpA) and perfluorononanoic acid (PFNA).

“The concerning thing about our results is that the strongest associations were not in the most studied legacy PFAS,” said lead author Jesse Goodrich, PhD, assistant professor at the Keck School of Medicine of USC. “They are among the newer PFAS, and we don’t have much information about their effect on human health.”

The researchers also examined whether inherited susceptibility to metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD), commonly called fatty liver disease, influenced cancer risk. They found that the association between PFHpA exposure and liver cancer was considerably stronger among participants with high genetic susceptibility to MASLD. No statistically significant association was detected among those with low susceptibility.

“Our study shows that genetic differences in how the liver processes fats may play an important role in determining susceptibility,” Goodrich said. “You have this one-two hit: first, your genes and then PFAS impacting this pathway.”

PFAS exposure may disrupt liver fat metabolism, contributing to the fat accumulation associated with MASLD. Over time, the condition can progress to inflammation, scarring, and cancer. MASLD is an increasingly important driver of HCC, which has a five-year survival rate below 20%.

“PFAS have been linked to an increase in fat accumulation in your liver, and over time, that can actually increase the risk of liver cancer,” Goodrich said.

PFAS are found in products such as nonstick cookware, food packaging, stain-resistant fabrics, and firefighting foams. Many resist degradation and persist in the environment for decades. These chemicals have been detected in drinking water across roughly half of U.S. water systems, while an estimated 99% of the global population has detectable PFAS in their blood.

Most regulatory attention has focused on older compounds such as perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) and perfluorooctanesulfonic acid (PFOS). PFHpA was developed as an alternative to these chemicals, which were phased out of many applications because of health and environmental concerns.

“PFOA and PFOS have received much of the scientific and regulatory attention, however, they represent only a small part of the PFAS family,” said senior author Vaia Lida Chatzi, MD, PhD, professor at the Keck School of Medicine. “Our findings show why we need to look beyond those legacy compounds. We can miss important associations with liver health if we study only the chemicals we already know best.”

The PFHpA finding also supports results from an independent National Cancer Institute study published two months earlier. However, these observational studies cannot establish that PFAS exposure causes liver cancer.

Identifying people with both elevated PFAS exposure and high genetic susceptibility could eventually help guide earlier liver cancer screening. Reducing exposure may also offer a potential prevention strategy, although its effect on cancer risk remains uncertain.

“Our study actually provides something that is actionable,” Goodrich said. “You can make lifestyle and diet changes and there are certain types of water filters you can put in that can reduce exposure. And if you have the information on genetic susceptibility, that could also provide additional evidence for things that you could do to mitigate risk.”

The study is the first publication from a USC Norris Comprehensive Cancer Center research program supported by a $3.4 million federal grant to investigate PFAS and liver cancer.

“This first paper from our NIH-funded study is an important step. Drawing on the diverse Multiethnic Cohort, it adds to the evidence that some PFAS may be associated with liver cancer,” said senior author V. Wendy Setiawan, PhD, professor at USC. “We hope this work will help build the evidence needed to reduce harmful exposures and inform prevention efforts for diverse communities.”

The team plans to investigate additional environmental exposures to better understand how chemicals encountered throughout life may contribute to cancer.

#6433. New Congress will still be filled with losers

The Capitol Dome is illuminated before dawn on Oct. 13. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

OPINION — Once again, the next Congress is going to be filled with losers.

This is not a personal judgment about their character or personality, but a simple recognition that many members have lost races before getting elected. And the incoming class is no different.

I’ve written many versions of this column for more than a decade, and yet the lesson always seems to get lost, no pun intended. Parties routinely attack candidates who enter a race with losses on their record. And, of course, it happened this cycle as well.

“We beat him once. We’ll beat him again,” National Republican Senatorial Committee Chairman Tim Scott declared when Democratic former Sen. Sherrod Brown announced his challenge to appointed GOP Sen. Jon Husted in the summer of 2025.

“Ohioans gladly sent him packing last year, and they’ll not hesitate to toss him aside again,” said a Republican strategist.

Brown lost reelection to Republican Bernie Moreno in 2024 but came back to defeat Husted for the state’s other Senate seat. And Brown is far from the only candidate to avenge a loss with an electoral victory last week.

The fact of the matter is that losing a race doesn’t have to be the end of a political career. Losses can lay the foundation for future success by building name ID or a fundraising network. Or sometimes it takes a change in the political environment or change in circumstances, such as running for an open seat instead of challenging an incumbent.

In addition to Brown, there are more than a dozen losers coming into the next Congress:

In some instances, though, the losses are piling up.

Republican Rep. John James of Michigan now has three statewide losses on his record. He lost Senate contests in 2018 (taking 46 percent of the vote) and 2020 (48 percent) and came up short in his bid for governor this year (44 percent).

Republican former Sen. John E. Sununu of New Hampshire, who lost reelection in 2008 to Democrat Jeanne Shaheen, fell in his comeback attempt for the open seat last week.

But they could take heart from another repeat loser. Charlie Crist, a former Florida governor and congressman, has had a handful of high-profile losses over the years, including for Senate and two gubernatorial comeback bids. He was just elected mayor of St. Petersburg.

So even though I know it’s a futile request, let’s have a bipartisan agreement not to attack candidates for past losses, because losing doesn’t mean they can’t later pull off a win.
